Book 5 · Ch.125.1 Ionizing radiation
Map 25.1 25.2 25.3 Summary

Section 25.1

Ionizing radiation

What radiation is, what makes some of it ionizing, how an X-ray tube works and what X-rays are used for, and why nuclear radiation is a different kind of thing from an X-ray beam.

Learning objectives

Students should be able to:

  • realise X-rays as ionizing electromagnetic radiations of short wavelengths with high penetrating power

    2022/31 MC

  • realise the emission of X-rays when fast electrons hit a heavy metal target

    2022/31 MC

  • discuss the uses of X-rays

    2022/31 MC

  • describe the origin and nature of α, β and γ radiations

    2015/31 MC2017/32 MCPP/34 MC2016/32 MC2017/10 LQ2014/10 LQ

  • realise the occurrence of radioactive decay in unstable nuclides

    2015/31 MC

ATwo types of radiation

Definition

Radiation is energy travelling from one place to another, either as an electromagnetic wave or as a stream of fast particles. It does not need a medium: light and X-rays cross a vacuum, and so do α and β particles.

Electromagnetic radiationParticle radiation
Oscillating E and B fields; no mass, no charge; speed \( c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \) in vacuumMoving particles with mass and kinetic energy; may carry charge; speed below \( c \)
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, γ raysElectron beams, α particles, β particles, neutrons
Both transfer energy. Both are radiation.

Concept check

Which of the following statements about radiation is/are correct?

  1. Radiation always requires a medium to travel in.
  2. Radiation transfers mass from one place to another.
  3. All electromagnetic waves are a form of radiation.

(3) is the definition: every EM wave carries energy from one place to another. (1) is false because EM waves and nuclear particles cross a vacuum; sunlight reaches us through empty space. (2) is false as a general statement: an EM wave transfers energy but no mass, and even a particle beam is described as radiation because of the energy it carries, not the mass.

BIonizing means knocking an electron out

Definition

Ionizing radiation carries enough energy per photon or per particle to remove an electron from an atom or molecule, turning it into an ion. Radiation that cannot do this is non-ionizing.

IonizingNon-ionizing
Energy per photon or particleEnough to knock an electron out of an atom or moleculeNot enough; at most the electron is raised to a higher energy level and falls back
ExamplesX-rays, γ rays, most ultraviolet; α and β particlesRadio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, the lowest-energy part of ultraviolet
HazardIons and broken bonds inside cells damage tissue and DNA; cells may die or become cancerousHeating at high intensity only; no ionization

Concept check

What does ionizing radiation do to an atom?

B is the definition of ionization. A describes excitation: the atom stays neutral, so nothing is ionized. C confuses ionization (an electron leaves the atom) with a nuclear change (the nucleus itself is altered). D describes non-ionizing radiation such as visible light.

CWhere the electromagnetic spectrum becomes ionizing

radiomicroIRvisUVX-raysGamma ray
non-ionizing split ionizing EM
  • Energy per photon rises with frequency (and falls with wavelength). Only photons above the ionization threshold can knock an electron out, so the ionizing part of the spectrum is the high-frequency, short-wavelength end.
  • The barrier lies far on the low-frequency side of ultraviolet: about one-tenth of the UV band is still non-ionizing; the rest of UV, all X-rays and all γ rays are ionizing.
  • Wavelength scale to remember: visible light \( \sim 5 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} \); X-rays \( \sim 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m} \), about the size of an atom, which is why they are so penetrating.

Concept check

On the electromagnetic spectrum, where does ionizing radiation begin?

B matches Fig. 25.5. A puts the barrier one band too high; sunburn and skin cancer from UV are ionizing damage. C and D put it too low: infrared and visible photons carry far too little energy to remove an electron, which is why a bright lamp or a heater is not a radiation hazard.

DHow an X-ray tube makes X-rays

Part of the tubeWhat it does
Heated filament (cathode)Emits electrons when hot, so a current can flow across the tube.
Very high voltage (tens of kV) between cathode and targetAccelerates the electrons to very high speed. A higher voltage gives electrons more kinetic energy and so more penetrating X-rays.
Vacuum inside the glassElectrons must not lose energy by colliding with air molecules on the way.
Heavy metal target (e.g. tungsten), angledElectrons are stopped abruptly; part of their kinetic energy is emitted as X-rays, which leave through the side of the tube.
Cooling (oil, rotating target)Only about 1% of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes X-rays; the rest heats the target.
Properties of X-rays

X-rays are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength (about \( 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m} \)). They carry no charge and no mass, travel at \( c \), are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields, pass through soft materials but are absorbed by dense ones, ionize atoms, blacken photographic film and cause some materials to fluoresce.

Concept check

(a) A beam of X-rays is a stream of fast-moving electrons.

The electrons stop in the target. What leaves the tube is an electromagnetic wave produced by the electrons' kinetic energy; it carries no charge, so an electric field cannot deflect it.

(b) X-rays are produced by bombarding a metal target with high-frequency electromagnetic waves.

The projectile is a fast electron, not a wave. The syllabus statement is "the emission of X-rays when fast electrons hit a heavy metal target".

(c) Exposure to X-rays is dangerous because they can damage cells.

X-rays are ionizing. The ions and broken bonds they create in cells damage tissue and DNA, so X-ray exposure is kept to a minimum and the radiographer stands behind a shield.

EUses of X-rays

UseWhich property is used
Medical imaging: bone fractures, teeth, chest; CT scans build a 3D image from many anglesPenetrating power differs with density: soft tissue transmits, bone and teeth absorb, so bone appears white on the developed film
Security screening of luggage; industrial inspection of welds, castings and pipes for hidden cracksHigh penetrating power through metal and plastic; dense objects cast a shadow
Radiotherapy: killing cancer cells with a focused high-energy beamIonizing: X-rays damage the DNA of the cells they pass through
Studying crystal structure (X-ray diffraction)Wavelength comparable to the spacing between atoms
Exam tip

Because X-rays are ionizing, every use comes with a precaution: the patient is exposed for the shortest time possible, sensitive areas are covered with a lead apron, and the radiographer stands behind a lead screen or leaves the room. Expect to be asked for both the use and the precaution.

Concept check

Which statement about X-rays is incorrect?

C is the false statement: an electric field only deflects charged particles, and X-rays carry no charge. A is how the tube works, B is their nature, and D is the key subtlety: ionization does not require the radiation itself to be charged, it requires enough energy per photon to remove an electron.

FWhich hit makes X-rays?

Concept check

In which set-up are X-rays produced?

Two conditions are needed: fast electrons as the projectile and a heavy metal target that stops them abruptly. A and B use a wave, not electrons, so they can at most warm or ionize the surface. C has electrons but a light, soft target that slows them gradually and produces essentially no X-rays.

GNuclear radiation is spontaneous; an X-ray beam is switched

Nuclear radiation (α, β, γ)X-rays
SourceThe nucleus of an unstable atom (a radioactive substance)Fast electrons stopped by a metal target in a tube
ControlSpontaneous and random: cannot be switched off, sped up or slowed down by heating, pressure or chemical changeSwitched on and off with the tube's power supply; intensity and penetrating power set by the current and voltage
Natureα: helium nucleus (2p + 2n). β: fast electron. γ: very high-frequency EM waveEM wave, like γ but produced outside the nucleus and usually of lower frequency
Definition

A substance is radioactive if it spontaneously emits α, β or γ radiation from unstable nuclei. The emission is called radioactive decay. The names α, β and γ were given before their nature was known; Section 25.2 explains what each one is.

Concept check

(a) All types of nuclear radiation are electromagnetic waves.

Only γ is an EM wave. α particles are helium nuclei and β particles are electrons; both have mass and charge.

(b) The emission of radiation from uranium can be switched on and off like an X-ray tube.

Decay is spontaneous. Nothing done to the atom from outside (heat, pressure, chemical reaction, electric field) changes when or whether its nucleus decays.

(c) Nuclear radiation is a kind of airborne material that can be spread from place to place by the wind.

The radiation itself is energy (particles or waves) travelling in straight lines from the nucleus. What wind can spread is radioactive material, the dust that contains the unstable nuclei. Keep "radiation" and "radioactive substance" separate.

Concept check

Which of the following nuclear reactions is/are spontaneous?

  1. β decay of sodium-24
  2. a boron nucleus absorbing an incoming neutron
  3. fusion of hydrogen isotopes in a reactor

"Spontaneous" means the nucleus changes on its own with nothing coming in. Only (1) qualifies: radioactive decay. (2) needs an incoming neutron and (3) needs the nuclei to be forced together at enormous temperature; both are induced reactions that stop when the supply of neutrons or heat stops.

Next: 25.2 Origin of nuclear radiation →

Section 25.2

Origin of nuclear radiation

The atom and its nucleus, how nuclides are written, what actually happens in α, β and γ decay, how to write and balance decay equations and follow a decay series, and where the background radiation around us comes from.

Learning objectives

Students should be able to:

  • describe the structure of an atom

  • define atomic number as the number of protons in the nucleus and mass number as the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom

    2012/36 MC2013/34 MC2021/31 MC

  • use symbolic notations to represent nuclides

    2013/34 MC2014/31 MC2020/31 MC2021/31 MC2025/32 MC2026/12 LQ

  • define isotope

    2012/36 MC2014/31 MC2020/31 MC

  • realise the existence of radioactive isotopes in some elements

    2021/33 MC

  • represent radioactive transmutations in α, β and γ decays using equations

    2013/34 MC2014/31 MC2020/31 MC2021/31 MC2025/32 MC2016/9 LQ2017/10 LQ2018/10 LQ2021/9 LQ2023/9 LQ2026/12 LQ

  • realise the occurrence of radioactive decay in unstable nuclides

    2015/31 MC

  • realise the existence of background radiation

    2021/33 MC2020/30 MC

  • suggest safety precautions in handling radioactive sources

    2015/32 MC2014/10 LQ

AStructure of the atom

proton neutron electron
ParticleWhereRelative massRelative charge
protonnucleus1+1
neutronnucleus10
electronshells around the nucleus≈ 1/1840 (negligible)−1
Definitions

Protons and neutrons are together called nucleons. The atomic number \( Z \) is the number of protons in the nucleus. The mass number \( A \) is the total number of nucleons, so the number of neutrons is \( N = A - Z \). A neutral atom has \( Z \) electrons, equal to its number of protons.

  • Almost all the mass is in the nucleus (nucleons are about 1840 times heavier than electrons) but almost all the volume is empty space: the atom is about \( 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m} \) across, the nucleus \( 10^{-15} \) to \( 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m} \). A nucleus in an atom is like a grain of sand in a football stadium.
  • The element is fixed by \( Z \) alone: every nucleus with 6 protons is carbon, whatever its number of neutrons.

Concept check

(a) The volume of an atom is mostly empty space.

The nucleus is about \( 10^{4} \) times smaller across than the atom, so it occupies about \( 10^{-12} \) of the atom's volume; the electrons are point-like. Almost everything in between is empty.

(b) Because the nucleus is so tiny, it holds only a small proportion of the atom's mass.

Size and mass are different things. One nucleon has about 1840 times the mass of an electron, so the nucleus holds more than 99.9% of the atom's mass in a tiny volume; it is extremely dense.

BNuclide notation and isotopes

¹H protium N = 0 · Z = 1

Definitions

A nuclide is a species of nucleus with a definite \( Z \) and \( A \), written \( {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \): mass number on top, atomic number below, e.g. \( {}^{12}_{6}\mathrm{C} \) or \( {}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \). Isotopes are nuclides of the same element (same \( Z \), same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons (different \( A \)).

  • Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties (same electrons) and slightly different physical properties (different mass). Natural carbon is about 99% \( {}^{12}\mathrm{C} \), 1% \( {}^{13}\mathrm{C} \) and a trace of \( {}^{14}\mathrm{C} \); only \( {}^{14}\mathrm{C} \) is radioactive. \( {}^{2}\mathrm{H} \) is called deuterium and \( {}^{3}\mathrm{H} \) tritium.
  • Some isotopes of every element are unstable. Nuclei with \( Z > 83 \) (heavier than bismuth) are all unstable: the strong nuclear force that binds nucleons acts only over a very short range, and in a large nucleus the electrical repulsion between the many protons wins.
Worked example

Three nuclides are \( {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{P} \), \( {}^{12}_{6}\mathrm{Q} \) and \( {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{R} \). (a) How many elements are present? (b) Which nuclide has the fewest neutrons? (c) Which neutral atoms have the fewest electrons?

  1. (a) The element is fixed by \( Z \). P and Q both have \( Z = 6 \) (isotopes of one element); R has \( Z = 7 \). Two elements.
  2. (b) \( N = A - Z \): P has 8, Q has 6, R has 7. Q has the fewest neutrons.
  3. (c) Electrons in a neutral atom equal \( Z \): P and Q have 6 each, R has 7. P and Q.

Concept check

Which graph best shows how the number of neutrons \( N \) in the nucleus varies with the mass number \( A \) for the isotopes of one element of atomic number \( Z \)?

For isotopes \( Z \) is fixed, so \( N = A - Z \): a straight line of slope 1 that meets the \( A \)-axis at \( A = Z \) (a nucleus with no neutrons). D. A passes through the origin, which would mean \( N = A \), forgetting the protons. B has \( N \) falling as \( A \) rises, impossible when each extra nucleon is a neutron. C keeps \( N \) constant while \( A \) changes, which would require \( Z \) to change, i.e. a different element.

Concept check

Consider the nuclides \( {}^{40}_{18}\mathrm{Ar} \), \( {}^{40}_{19}\mathrm{K} \), \( {}^{40}_{20}\mathrm{Ca} \) and \( {}^{42}_{20}\mathrm{Ca} \). Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. \( {}^{40}\mathrm{Ar} \), \( {}^{40}\mathrm{K} \) and \( {}^{40}\mathrm{Ca} \) are isotopes because they have the same mass number.
  2. \( {}^{40}\mathrm{Ca} \) and \( {}^{42}\mathrm{Ca} \) are isotopes.
  3. \( {}^{40}\mathrm{Ar} \) and \( {}^{42}\mathrm{Ca} \) have the same number of neutrons.

Isotopes share \( Z \), not \( A \). (1) is the classic trap: three different elements happen to have \( A = 40 \); they are not isotopes. (2) is correct: same \( Z = 20 \), different \( A \). (3): \( N = 40 - 18 = 22 \) for argon-40 and \( 42 - 20 = 22 \) for calcium-42, so it is also correct. Answer C.

CThree ways an unstable nucleus sheds energy

Vocabulary

An unstable nuclide (a radionuclide or radioisotope) gets rid of excess energy by emitting radiation; this is radioactive decay. The original nucleus is the parent, the nucleus left behind is the daughter. When the daughter is a different element (different \( Z \)) the change is a transmutation. Decay is spontaneous and random: nothing outside the nucleus (heat, pressure, chemical bonding) starts, stops, speeds or slows it.

DecayWhat leavesWhat happens inside the nucleusChange in \( A \)Change in \( Z \)Change in \( N \)
αA helium nucleus \( {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \): 2 protons + 2 neutronsA tightly bound group of four nucleons is ejected−4−2−2
βA fast electron \( {}^{0}_{-1}e \) (also written \( {}^{0}_{-1}\beta \))One neutron turns into a proton, which stays, and an electron, which is emitted. The electron is created in the nucleus; it is not one of the orbital electrons0+1−1
γA very high-frequency EM wave, no mass, no chargeAfter an α or β decay the daughter is often left with excess energy (an excited nucleus, marked *). It drops to its normal state by emitting the energy as a γ ray000
  • Conservation. In every equation the total mass number and the total atomic number (charge) are the same on both sides. This is how you balance an unknown.
  • Consequences. Any α or β decay produces a different element, so it is always a transmutation. γ emission changes neither \( A \) nor \( Z \); the nuclide only loses energy. That is why a source such as Ra-226 or Am-241 is listed as emitting "α and γ": the γ follows the α from the excited daughter.
  • Answer format. If asked "state the kind of radiation", write "α particle" or "β particle", not "α decay". In β decay the particle emitted is an electron; no neutron is emitted.
Worked example

Write the equation for (a) the α decay of radium-226 (\( Z = 88 \)) to radon, and (b) the β decay of carbon-14 (\( Z = 6 \)) to nitrogen.

  1. (a) Put the parent on the left, the daughter and the particle on the right; balance top and bottom: \( 226 = A + 4 \) gives \( A = 222 \); \( 88 = Z + 2 \) gives \( Z = 86 \).
    \[ {}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \rightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \]
  2. (b) The electron has \( A = 0 \), \( Z = -1 \): \( 14 = A + 0 \) gives \( A = 14 \); \( 6 = Z + (-1) \) gives \( Z = 7 \).
    \[ {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}e \]

Concept check

Which equation correctly represents the β decay of lead-214, \( {}^{214}_{82}\mathrm{Pb} \)?

B: the electron is emitted (right-hand side) and the totals balance: \( 214 = 214 + 0 \), \( 82 = 83 + (-1) \). A puts the electron on the left as if it were absorbed. C lowers \( A \), but an electron has zero mass number. D lowers \( Z \), forgetting that the electron's charge is −1, so the daughter must have one more proton.

Concept check

A nuclide R undergoes β decay, and the daughter then emits a γ ray. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. After the β decay the nucleus has one more proton and one fewer neutron.
  2. The β particle is one of the orbital electrons of the atom R.
  3. The γ emission leaves the mass number and atomic number unchanged.

(1) is what β decay is: a neutron becomes a proton plus an electron, so \( Z \) rises by 1, \( N \) falls by 1 and \( A \) is unchanged. (3) is right: a γ ray carries away energy only. (2) is the common misconception; the electron is created inside the nucleus at the moment of decay. Answer C.

Write it out

Bismuth-213 (\( Z = 83 \)) undergoes β decay to polonium (Po), which then undergoes α decay to lead (Pb). Write the two decay equations. (HKDSE 2026 Paper 1B Q12, 2 marks)

\[ {}^{213}_{83}\mathrm{Bi} \rightarrow {}^{213}_{84}\mathrm{Po} + {}^{0}_{-1}e \]
\[ {}^{213}_{84}\mathrm{Po} \rightarrow {}^{209}_{82}\mathrm{Pb} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \]

One mark for each equation with both numbers correct on every symbol. Check each line: top row 213 = 213 + 0 and 213 = 209 + 4; bottom row 83 = 84 − 1 and 84 = 82 + 2.

DDecay series

The daughter of a decay is often itself unstable and decays again. The chain continues until a stable nuclide is reached. Uranium-238 goes through 14 decays (8 α and 6 β) before ending at stable lead-206: \( {}^{238}\mathrm{U} \xrightarrow{\alpha} {}^{234}\mathrm{Th} \xrightarrow{\beta} {}^{234}\mathrm{Pa} \xrightarrow{\beta} {}^{234}\mathrm{U} \xrightarrow{\alpha} \cdots \rightarrow {}^{206}\mathrm{Pb} \). Members of a series with the same \( Z \) are isotopes of one another.

DecayOn an \( A \)-\( Z \) chartOn an \( N \)-\( Z \) chart
αdown 4, left 2down 2, left 2 (diagonal)
βright 1, same heightdown 1, right 1 (diagonal the other way)
γno move: the point stays where it is
Worked example: counting α and β

Plutonium-239 decays through a series to lead-207. How many α and how many β decays are involved?

\[ {}^{239}_{94}\mathrm{Pu} \rightarrow {}^{207}_{82}\mathrm{Pb} \]
  1. Only α changes \( A \), by 4 each time: \(\Delta A = 239 - 207 = 32\) → nα = 32 / 4 = 8
  2. Those 8 α alone would take \( Z \) to \( 94 - 2 \times 8 = 78 \).
  3. Each β raises \( Z \) by 1 and the final \( Z \) is 82, so nβ = 82 − 78 = 4

Write it in exam form as two equations: \( 4n_{\alpha} = \Delta A \) and \( 2n_{\alpha} - n_{\beta} = \Delta Z \).

Exam tip: which nuclides can belong to a series?

Because only α changes \( A \), and by 4 each time, every member of a series has a mass number that differs from the parent's by a multiple of 4. A candidate with the wrong \( A \) can be ruled out immediately. Then check \( Z \): after \( n_{\alpha} \) alphas and \( n_{\beta} \) betas, \( Z = Z_0 - 2n_{\alpha} + n_{\beta} \) with \( n_{\beta} \geq 0 \). Also: "state the end product of the Ra-226 series from Pb-206, Pb-207, Pb-208" is answered by \( 226 - 206 = 20 \), a multiple of 4.

Concept check

Neptunium-237, \( {}^{237}_{93}\mathrm{Np} \), decays through a series to stable bismuth-209, \( {}^{209}_{83}\mathrm{Bi} \). The numbers of α and β decays are

\( \Delta A = 237 - 209 = 28 = 4 \times 7 \), so 7 α. After them \( Z = 93 - 14 = 79 \); to reach 83 needs 4 β. B. A and D get the α count wrong (28 is not 24 or 32). C subtracts the \( Z \) values directly (\( 93 - 83 = 10 \), then confuses the bookkeeping) instead of first applying the α step.

Concept check

A uranium-238 nucleus \( {}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \) undergoes an α decay, then two β decays, then another α decay, to become nuclide X. What are the atomic number and mass number of X?

Two α: \( A \) falls by 8 to 230 and \( Z \) by 4 to 88. Two β: \( Z \) rises by 2 to 90, \( A \) unchanged. So (90, 230), A. B and D forget the second α in \( A \); C forgets that β raises \( Z \).

Concept check

A nuclide W decays as follows: W → X (α decay), X → Y (β decay), Y → Z (β decay). Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. X has one more proton than Y.
  2. W has two more neutrons than X.
  3. W and Z are isotopes.

Track \( (Z, N) \). α: \( (Z-2, N-2) \); each β: \( (Z+1, N-1) \). So X = \( (Z-2, N-2) \), Y = \( (Z-1, N-3) \), Z = \( (Z, N-4) \). (1) X has one fewer proton than Y, false. (2) true: W has two more neutrons than X. (3) true: W and Z have the same \( Z \) (and \( A \) differs by 4), so they are isotopes. Answer D.

Concept check

Radium-226, \( {}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \), decays by a series of α and β decays. Which of the following nuclides cannot be a member of its series?

\( A \) must fall in steps of 4 from 226. B has \( 226 - 216 = 10 \), not a multiple of 4, so it is impossible whatever the β count. The others pass: A is one α; C is 3 α (\( Z = 82 \)) then 1 β; D is 4 α (\( Z = 80 \)) then 2 β. (This is the reasoning behind HKDSE 2025 Paper 1A Q32.)

Concept check

A school radium-226 source is described as an α emitter, yet a detector near it also registers β and γ radiation. The best explanation is that

B. Ra-226 is part of the U-238 series; its daughters Rn-222, Po-218, Pb-214, Bi-214 and so on accumulate inside the sealed source and several of them are β or γ emitters. The examiners' report for this question singled out A as the wrong answer many candidates gave. C describes no real process, and D cannot explain readings far above background.

ERadioactive sources in the laboratory and how to handle them

  • Schools may use only weak sealed sources like this one. Radioactive material that is not enclosed (rock samples, radon gas) is an open source.
  • Radiation from the source cannot make the room, the bench or the student radioactive (see irradiation vs contamination in Section F). The danger is the dose of ionizing radiation absorbed while the source is out.
Common school sourceRadiation emitted
Radium-226α, β and γ (β and much of the γ come from daughters in its series)
Americium-241α and a small amount of γ
Strontium-90β
Cobalt-60β and γ (the β from Co-60, the γ from the excited Ni-60 daughter); used as a γ source behind an absorber
PrecautionReason
Handle only with long forceps or tongs; never touch with fingersDistance: the radiation intensity falls off with distance from the source, and α and β have short ranges in air
Keep the window pointed away from people, especially the eyesRadiation leaves the case only through the window; the eye lens is easily damaged
Return the source promptly to its lead-lined box; keep the box locked and labelled with the radiation warning sign (trefoil)Lead absorbs the radiation, including γ; the lock and label prevent accidental exposure. A wooden or plastic box is not acceptable
Minimise the time the source is outDose absorbed is proportional to exposure time
Wash hands after the experiment; never eat or drink in the laboratoryRemoves any contamination; prevents radioactive material entering the body, where α is most damaging
Inside vs outside the body

Outside the body γ is the most dangerous: it penetrates to internal organs, while α is stopped by a few centimetres of air or the dead outer layer of skin. Inside the body (breathed in or swallowed) α is the most dangerous: it is the strongest ionizer and dumps all its energy into the surrounding cells. This reversal is why radon gas is a hazard (Section F) and why α is never used as a medical tracer (Chapter 26).

Concept check

A teacher takes a sealed γ source out of its box for a demonstration. Which of the following precautions is/are justified by the reason given?

  1. Hold the source with long forceps, because the intensity received falls with distance from the source.
  2. Store the source in a thick wooden box, because wood absorbs γ rays well.
  3. Keep the demonstration short, because the dose absorbed increases with exposure time.

(1) and (3) are the two principles that appear in every marking scheme: distance and time. (2) fails on the reason: γ passes through wood almost unhindered; the box must be lead-lined. Answer C.

Concept check

A source emits α and γ radiation. Which type of radiation is the more dangerous (i) if the source is accidentally swallowed, and (ii) if the sealed source is held in the hand?

B. Inside the body nothing shields the tissue from the α, which is the strongest ionizer, so α does the most damage. In the hand the α is stopped by the metal case or by the skin and does nothing, while γ passes through the hand and into the body. A and D ignore the location; C reverses the logic.

FBackground radiation

A detector registers ionizing radiation even with no source in the room. This background radiation comes mostly from natural sources and reaches everyone, everywhere, all the time. In Hong Kong a GM counter typically reads about 1 count per second from background; the average annual dose is about 2.4 mSv, which is far too low to cause any apparent harm.

SourceWhat it is and what affects it
RadonA colourless, odourless radioactive gas produced in the U-238 decay series in rocks and soil. It seeps out of the ground and out of granite and concrete building materials and collects in poorly ventilated rooms. Being a gas it is inhaled, and it and its daughters emit α inside the lungs. The remedy is ventilation (open windows), not sealing the room or wearing a dust mask.
Rocks and soilRadioactive minerals (uranium, thorium, potassium-40) present since the Earth formed. Granite areas and caves have higher background than the open air above them.
Cosmic raysVery energetic particles from space. The atmosphere shields us, so the dose is higher on mountains and in aircraft (airline crews receive a measurably larger dose) and lower deep inside a cave or mine.
Food, drink, the bodyAll living things contain a little potassium-40 and carbon-14; so does sea water. Every human body is slightly radioactive.
ArtificialMedical X-rays and radiotherapy (by far the largest artificial share), industrial sources, consumer products such as smoke detectors, fallout from past nuclear weapon tests, and any leakage from nuclear power stations. Note that leakage counts as artificial background.
Irradiation vs contamination

An object that has been irradiated has only absorbed the energy of the radiation; it does not become radioactive. A patient after an X-ray, luggage after a security scan, or a wrapped film that has darkened under a source are irradiated, not radioactive. An object is contaminated when radioactive material itself gets onto or into it; it then goes on emitting radiation until the material is removed or decays. Washing hands after handling a source removes possible contamination.

Concept check

Which of the following may contain sources of ionizing radiation?

  1. sea water
  2. a rock sample
  3. the human body

All three, D. Radioactive isotopes of common elements (potassium-40, carbon-14, uranium and thorium traces) are present in rock, dissolved in sea water and inside our own tissues. Fewer than half of candidates chose this in 2021; the trap is to think "radioactive" means "unusual".

Concept check

With no source nearby, a GM counter reads about 30 counts per minute. A student then holds a mobile phone that is making a call next to the tube. Which statement is correct?

B. A GM tube counts ionizing events; microwaves cannot ionize argon atoms, so the phone is invisible to it. A is impossible: background is always present, so a GM counter never reads zero. C confuses "radiation" with "ionizing radiation". D has no mechanism.

Concept check

A GM counter shows a higher background count inside a cave than in the open air outside it. Which source is least likely to be responsible for the increase?

C. The rock above a cave shields it from cosmic rays, so the cosmic contribution is lower underground, not higher. Rock, soil and trapped radon all raise the count. The reverse question, "why is background higher on a mountain top?", has the answer cosmic rays: less atmosphere above to absorb them.

Concept check

(a) After a chest X-ray a patient is slightly radioactive for a few hours.

The patient was irradiated: the X-rays deposited energy and left. No radioactive material was put into the body, so nothing goes on emitting. Contamination requires the radioactive substance itself.

(b) The best way to reduce the radon level in a flat is to keep the windows closed so that no radon can enter from outside.

Radon comes from the building materials and the ground beneath the flat, and a closed room lets it accumulate. Ventilation dilutes it with outside air, where the level is low.

(c) Background radiation varies from place to place.

Granite regions, high altitude and poorly ventilated basements all give higher readings; the sea surface gives lower. This is why a background reading must be taken at the place and time of every experiment.

Book 5 · Ch.125.3 Properties and detection
Map 25.1 25.2 25.3 Summary

Section 25.3

Properties and detection of nuclear radiation

How α, β and γ ionize, how each detector turns that ionization into something visible, how far each radiation travels and what stops it, how to identify an unknown source from absorber readings, and how electric and magnetic fields separate the three.

Learning objectives

Students should be able to:

  • compare α, β and γ radiations in terms of their penetrating power, ranges, ionizing power, behaviour in electric field and magnetic field, and cloud chamber tracks

    2014/32 MC2016/32 MC2017/31 MC2017/32 MC2019/31 MCPP/34 MCPP/35 MCSAP/36 MC2014/10 LQ

  • detect radiation with a photographic film and GM counter

    2017/32 MC2014/32 MC2015/32 MCPP/35 MCSAP/36 MC

  • detect radiation in terms of count rate using a GM counter

    2014/32 MC2019/31 MC2020/30 MCPP/35 MCSAP/36 MC

AIonizing power

NatureSpeedRelative massChargeIon-pairs per cm of airIonizing power
αhelium nucleusup to about 0.05\( c \) (some sources say 0.1\( c \))4 (≈ 7200 × electron)+220 000 to 50 000strongest
βfast electronup to 0.98\( c \)1/1840−150 to 500weaker
γEM wave\( c \)005 to 8weakest
  • Why α ionizes most. It is slow, massive and carries two units of charge, so it spends a long time near each atom it passes and pulls strongly on the electrons. β is light, fast and singly charged; γ has no charge at all and ionizes only when it happens to be absorbed by an electron.
  • All three can ionize, γ included; the differences are in how many pairs per centimetre. Because it loses energy at every ionization, the strongest ionizer runs out of energy first: ionizing power and range go opposite ways (Section F).
  • Nothing is ionized in a vacuum: there are no atoms to ionize. Ionizing radiation is not only nuclear radiation; X-rays ionize too.

Concept check

Which of the following statements about α, β and γ radiation is/are correct?

  1. The ionizing power of α particles is much stronger than that of β particles.
  2. γ rays can be completely shielded by 10 cm of concrete.
  3. α, β and γ radiation are all deflected by an electric field.

(1) is right by two orders of magnitude (Table 25.4). (2) is the classic γ trap: dense material reduces γ intensity (each thickness cuts it by a fixed fraction) but never stops it completely, so "completely shielded" is wrong. (3) fails for γ, which carries no charge. Answer A.

BIonized air conducts

Air is normally an insulator. Ionizing radiation gives it free charge carriers, so it conducts. Everything in this section follows from that single fact.

Change madeEffect on the current, and why
Replace the α source by a β source of similar activityCurrent falls: β makes far fewer ion-pairs per centimetre.
Move the α source slowly away from the platesCurrent falls to zero within a few centimetres: α has a range of only about 5 cm in air, so beyond that no air between the plates is ionized.
Pump the air out of the space between the platesCurrent falls to zero. There is nothing to ionize, so there are no charge carriers, even though the α now travels further.
Blow smoke between the platesCurrent falls: smoke particles capture the ions, making heavy, slow carriers. This is how an ionization smoke detector triggers its alarm (Chapter 26).
Bring the source near a charged metal sphere or a charged electroscopeThe sphere discharges and the leaf falls, whatever the sign of its charge: ions of the opposite sign are drawn to it and neutralise it.
Exam tip

It is the ions in the air that neutralise a charged object or carry the current, not the α particles themselves. "The α particles are attracted to the charged dust and neutralise it" was the wrong answer picked out in the examiners' report for HKDSE 2017 Paper 1B Q10 (the anti-static brush).

Concept check

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. An α particle is heavier than a β particle.
  2. α particles have a stronger penetrating power than β particles.
  3. An α source held near a positively charged metal sphere can discharge the sphere.

(1): an α particle (two protons, two neutrons) is about 7200 times heavier than an electron. (3): the α ionizes the air; the negative ions are attracted to the positive sphere and neutralise it. A negatively charged sphere would be discharged just as well by the positive ions. (2) is backwards: α is the strongest ionizer and therefore the least penetrating. Answer C.

Concept check

In Fig. 25.26 the α source is moved slowly away from the plates. How does the meter reading change?

C. Once the source is further from the plates than the range of the α particles, none of them reach the air between the plates, so no ion-pairs are formed there. D would describe a β source (range of a few metres). A ignores range; B has no mechanism. In a vacuum the current would be zero at any distance.

CCloud chamber tracks

How the chamber works

Dry ice cools the base of the chamber. A felt ring soaked in alcohol near the top fills the chamber with alcohol vapour, which becomes supersaturated in the cold layer near the base. Radiation passing through ionizes the air along its path, and the vapour condenses on the ions into droplets. Lit from the side, the line of droplets shows up as a white track. Because tracks appear at random places and at random moments, the chamber is also direct evidence that decay is random.

AppearanceWhy
αThick, straight, short (a few cm) and all about the same lengthThick because it is a strong ionizer (many droplets per cm). Straight because it is massive and is not knocked off course by collisions with air molecules. Short because it spends its energy quickly. Equal lengths because the α particles from one source are emitted with the same energy.
βThin, twisted, longerThin because it ionizes weakly. Twisted because it is light and is deflected in every collision.
γScattered, faint, short wisps, hardly observableγ itself leaves almost no ions; the few visible tracks are made by electrons it knocks out of atoms.
  • The cloud chamber is the only common detector that can tell the three radiations apart on its own. Film and a GM counter show that radiation is present and how much; they cannot say which kind without absorbers or a field.
  • Background radiation also makes tracks: a chamber with no source still shows occasional tracks.
  • In a magnetic field the tracks curve; the direction of curvature gives the sign of the charge and the radius gives the momentum.
  • In a chamber filled with helium, an α track sometimes forks at a right angle: the α made an oblique elastic collision with a helium nucleus of equal mass, and equal masses separate at 90°. This is evidence that the α particle is a helium nucleus.

Concept check

α tracks in a cloud chamber are thick and straight. Which of the following properties of α particles explain this?

  1. They are heavy.
  2. They have strong ionizing power.
  3. They have weak penetrating power.

Thick comes from (2): many ion-pairs per cm means many droplets. Straight comes from (1): a heavy particle is not deflected by the light air molecules it hits. (3) explains why the track is short, not why it is thick or straight, so it is not a reason for the property asked. Answer C.

Concept check

Which of the following detectors, used on its own, can distinguish α, β and γ radiation?

  1. photographic film
  2. cloud chamber
  3. GM counter

Only the cloud chamber shows a different track for each radiation. Film darkens and a GM tube counts whatever ionizing radiation reaches them; to identify the type you must add absorbers (Section G) or a field (Section H). Answer B.

DPhotographic film and the film badge

  • Film detects radiation because ionizing radiation blackens photographic film just as light does. Becquerel discovered radioactivity this way in 1896. A classic demonstration: a key or coin is laid on a film wrapped in black paper and a β source is held above it; after developing, the film is dark except for a white shadow of the key. The radiation passed through the paper but not the metal. The paper envelope has been irradiated but is not radioactive.
  • Purpose of the badge. Worn by radiation workers to record the total (cumulative) dose received over weeks. Darker film means a stronger source or a longer exposure. It is cheap and simple but approximate, and it can only be read after the fact.
  • The wrapper keeps visible light out; otherwise the film would blacken anyway. The same wrapper stops all α particles, so a film badge can never detect α. This was the point of HKDSE 2015 Paper 1A Q32, which only 35% of candidates got right.
Radiation reaching the badgeDeveloped film
β onlyDark under the open window only; the aluminium and lead regions stay clear (5 mm Al stops β)
γ onlyAll three regions dark; lead region a little lighter than the others
β and γOpen window darkest (β + γ); aluminium region dark (γ); lead region lightest (part of the γ)
α onlyNo darkening anywhere: the wrapper stops α before it reaches the film

Concept check

A worker's film badge is wrapped in opaque plastic. Which type of radiation can the badge not monitor?

A. α is stopped by a sheet of paper, so the light-proof wrapper alone absorbs it and nothing reaches the film. β passes the wrapper and darkens the open-window region; γ darkens every region. Most candidates chose C, thinking γ is "too penetrating to be caught", but γ is partly absorbed by the film and blackens it.

Write it out

A film badge has an open window, a 5 mm aluminium sheet and a 5 mm lead sheet in front of a wrapped film. Describe the appearance of the developed film if the wearer was exposed to (i) β only, (ii) γ only. Why is the film wrapped? (4 marks)

  1. (i) Only the region behind the open window is darkened; the aluminium and lead regions stay clear because 5 mm of aluminium (and lead) stops β.
  2. (ii) All three regions are darkened, the lead region least, because γ passes through aluminium almost unchanged and is only partly absorbed by lead.
  3. The wrapper stops visible light from blackening the film, so any darkening is due to the ionizing radiation alone.

Pattern of darkening (1 mark each case), the absorber reason (1), the wrapper reason (1).

EThe Geiger-Müller counter and count rate

How a GM counter works, step by step
  1. The tube contains argon at low pressure. A high voltage is kept between the central wire (positive, the anode) and the metal case (negative, the cathode). One end is a thin mica window.
  2. Radiation enters through the window and ionizes argon atoms, producing ion-pairs.
  3. The electrons are accelerated to the wire and the positive ions to the case; on the way they ionize more atoms, so a brief pulse of current flows through the tube.
  4. Each pulse is counted by the attached scaler (total count) or ratemeter (counts per second or per minute, the count rate).
\[ \text{corrected count rate} = \text{recorded count rate} - \text{background count rate} \]
  • Always measure the background first, with the source locked away, because every reading includes it. Decay is random, so readings fluctuate; take several readings and average them.
  • A GM counter never reads zero: background is always present. In Hong Kong a typical background is about 1 count per second (30 to 60 counts per minute).
  • Because it counts ion-pairs, the tube detects α and β more efficiently than γ, which usually passes straight through without ionizing anything. To detect α the plastic grid must be removed and the source placed within about 1.5 cm of the window; β and γ sources are placed about 5 cm away.
  • A GM counter is faster and more precise than film, but on its own it cannot tell which type of radiation it is counting.
  • The corrected count rate is proportional to the activity of the source (Chapter 26) but much smaller than it: the source radiates in all directions and the tube catches only the small fraction that enters its window, and some of that is absorbed on the way.

Concept check

With no radioactive source in the laboratory, a GM counter gives readings of 46, 58, 41, 55 and 50 counts per 100 s in five successive trials. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. The counter is faulty, because it should read zero without a source.
  2. The readings differ because radioactive decay is a random process.
  3. The best estimate of the background count rate is the mean, about 0.5 counts per second.

(1) is wrong: background radiation from radon, rocks, cosmic rays and the body reaches the tube everywhere, so a non-zero reading is normal. (2) and (3) are the two things to write about any set of background readings: the scatter is randomness, and averaging reduces its effect. Answer D.

FRange and penetrating power

Unknown source
Absorbers in place 0 cpm

Definitions

The range of a radiation in a material is the distance it travels before it has lost all its energy and stops. Penetrating power is the ability to pass through material. A strong ionizer loses energy quickly, so strong ionizing power means short range and weak penetrating power: α < β < γ in penetrating power, the reverse of Table 25.4.

Range in airStopped byPenetrating power
αa few cm (about 5 cm)a sheet of paper, the skin, a few cm of airweakest
βa few m (about 5 m)about 5 mm of aluminium; the count falls gradually as the aluminium thickensstrong
γvery long (about 100 m, falling off with distance rather than stopping)never completely stopped: 25 mm of lead roughly halves the intensity, and each further 25 mm halves it againstrongest
Experiment: measuring the range of α in air
  1. With the source locked away, record the background count rate.
  2. Remove the plastic grid from the GM tube and line up the α source with the window, a few millimetres away. Record the count rate.
  3. Move the source away in small steps, recording the count rate each time, until the reading falls to the background value. Measure the separation with a metre rule: this is the range.
  4. On a graph of count rate against distance the curve drops and then levels off; the level part is background and the distance at which it is reached is the range. To rule out gravity as the reason the α "stop", repeat with the apparatus turned through 90°: the result is the same.
Worked example: γ through thick lead

A γ source gives 275 counts per minute at a GM tube; the background is 30 counts per minute. Estimate the reading with 100 mm of lead between source and tube, given that 25 mm of lead halves the γ intensity.

  1. Count from the source alone: \( 275 - 30 = 245 \) counts per minute.
  2. 100 mm is four thicknesses of 25 mm, so the source count is halved four times: \( 245 / 2^{4} \approx 15 \) counts per minute.
  3. Add the background back: reading \( \approx 15 + 30 = 45 \) counts per minute. It can never fall below 30.

Concept check

A GM tube is placed at increasing distances \( d \) from a source. The count rate falls steadily and from \( d = 4\ \mathrm{cm} \) onwards stays at about 28 counts per minute however far the tube is moved. Which conclusion is correct?

C. A reading that levels off and stays constant at large distance is the background (a source never reads below it). The radiation from the source stops arriving at 4 cm, a few centimetres, which is the range of α in air. β would reach several metres and γ would fall off only slowly, so A and B are out. D confuses the source with what reaches the detector: decay is not affected by where the tube is.

GIdentifying the radiation from absorber readings

The standard test: place the source in front of a GM tube and insert, in turn, a sheet of paper, about 5 mm of aluminium and about 25 mm of lead. Each absorber stops one more type. Compare each reading with the one before it and with the background.

How to write the answer: observation, reasoning, conclusion

For Example 25.6, one line per absorber:

  1. Paper: no significant change (700 → 700). Paper stops α. So the source emits no α.
  2. 5 mm aluminium: large drop (700 → 315). Aluminium stops β (and would stop α). So the source emits β.
  3. 25 mm lead: further drop (315 → 190) but still well above background (61). Lead only partly absorbs γ. So the source emits γ.
  4. Conclusion: β and γ, no α.
The hard cases

No paper step. 5 mm Al stops both α and β, so a drop at aluminium without a paper reading means "α or β or both", not "β". Lead only. A drop from air to 5 mm Pb proves nothing about which of α or β is present; a further drop from 5 mm to 15 mm Pb proves γ, and the background must be below the final reading. Background not given. If the reading keeps roughly halving as the lead thickens (say 90 → 46 from 25 to 50 mm), it has not reached a flat floor, so γ is still being absorbed and is present. Proving "X only". You need no significant drop at the other steps and a final reading at background. Repeated readings in a table (e.g. 210, 227; 224, 215) differ by randomness; a change only counts if it is well outside that scatter.

Concept check

A source emits α, β and γ radiation. A piece of cardboard, then a 5 mm aluminium sheet, then a 10 mm lead sheet are placed in a line in front of it. Detectors X, Y and Z are placed just after the cardboard, the aluminium and the lead respectively. Which statement is correct?

Cardboard stops α, so α reaches nowhere (C wrong). β passes cardboard and reaches X, but 5 mm Al stops it, so it never reaches Y or Z: D is correct and B wrong. γ passes everything, reduced but present at Z (A wrong).

Concept check

A source emits α and γ radiation. With no absorber the GM counter records 450 counts per minute; the background is 50 counts per minute. A piece of cardboard, a 1 mm aluminium sheet and a 2 mm lead sheet are then inserted in turn (one at a time), giving corrected count rates \( x \), \( y \) and \( z \). Which set of values is possible?

Corrected rate with no absorber is \( 450 - 50 = 400 \), all from α and γ. Cardboard removes all the α and none of the γ; 1 mm Al does the same, so \( x = y \) (the γ part). 2 mm Pb absorbs some γ, so \( z \) is smaller than \( y \) but not zero. Only A fits. B has aluminium removing something extra, which would need β. C has lead stopping γ completely. D has aluminium and lead doing different things to what is left after the cardboard, but there is no β to remove.

Concept check

Count rates (per second) measured with absorbers between a source and a GM tube: none 400; paper 398; 5 mm Al 180; 25 mm Pb 90; 50 mm Pb 46. The background was not measured. The source emits

Paper: no drop, so no α (D out). Aluminium: a large drop, so β is present (B out). Lead: the count halves again between 25 mm and 50 mm, so it is not sitting at a flat background floor; something is still being attenuated, which must be γ (A out). Answer C. This is how to reason when the background is not given: a reading that keeps changing with thickness is not background.

Concept check

With a source in front of a GM tube the readings are: no absorber 504; 5 mm lead 261; 15 mm lead 157 (counts per minute). No other absorbers were used. Which of the following can be concluded?

  1. The source emits β.
  2. The source emits γ.
  3. The background count rate is about 157 counts per minute.

Only (2). The drop from 261 to 157 as the lead thickens shows γ is present. The first drop (504 → 261) could be α, β or both being stopped by the 5 mm lead, so (1) is not proved. (3) is wrong because 15 mm of lead does not stop γ; the background is somewhere below 157. Answer B.

Concept check

A spark counter sparks when a radium-226 source is held close to its wire gauze. A student claims that the sparks are caused by the α particles rather than by the β or γ that the source also emits. Which test best verifies this claim?

B: a test that removes only the α (paper, or distance beyond its range) and nothing else. If the sparks stop, the α were responsible. A shows what the source emits but not what causes the sparks; the examiners' report noted that many candidates gave this answer. C barely affects α and is inconclusive. D changes the detector, not the radiation.

Write it out

A source is placed 10 cm from a GM tube. Two readings are taken with each absorber (counts per minute): no absorber 210, 227; paper 224, 215; 5 mm Al 45, 47; 10 mm Pb 48, 42. The background is about 45 counts per minute. Show that the source emits β only. (6 marks)

  1. Paper. Observation: no significant change (about 220 both times; the two repeat readings differ by about as much). Reasoning: paper stops α. Conclusion: no α is emitted.
  2. 5 mm aluminium. Observation: large drop to about 46. Reasoning: aluminium stops β. Conclusion: β is emitted.
  3. 10 mm lead. Observation: no further drop; the reading (about 45) equals the background. Reasoning: lead would reduce γ but there is nothing above background left to reduce. Conclusion: no γ is emitted.

Each absorber earns an observation mark and a reasoning-plus-conclusion mark. The "β only" claim needs all three lines: what paper did not do, what aluminium did, and that lead found nothing left.

HElectric and magnetic fields separate the three

Electric fieldMagnetic field
α (+2, heavy)Force along \( E \), towards the negative plate; small deflectionFleming's left-hand rule with the current in the direction of motion; small deflection
β (−1, light)Force against \( E \), towards the positive plate; large deflectionFleming's left-hand rule with the current opposite to the motion (negative charge); large deflection, opposite side to α
γ (no charge)No force, no deflection
  • Why β bends more. Not because of a larger force: the force on an α is twice as large (charge 2e against e). The β is deflected far more because its mass is about 1/7200 of the α's, so the same order of force gives it a far greater acceleration. The degree of deflection depends on mass, charge magnitude and speed; the sign of the charge only fixes the side.
  • The collimator (two lead blocks with a narrow slit) turns the radiation leaving the source in all directions into a fine beam travelling in one direction, so that a deflection can be seen. If film is the detector, the apparatus must be in the dark.
  • β spreads out. β particles leave a source with a range of speeds, so they are deflected by different amounts and fan out over a region instead of hitting one spot. A GM tube at one point therefore catches only some of them, and the total β count with the field on is less than with it off. α particles from one source all have nearly the same speed, so they stay together.
  • In air the α is absorbed within a few centimetres and is usually missing from the picture; to see the α path the apparatus must be evacuated.
  • Reading a detector scan. Place γ at the undeflected position, β on the side the rule predicts, α (if any) on the other side. Two positions with equal small counts are both reading background. A missing peak does not prove a radiation is absent if it was deflected off the line of the scan or absorbed before arriving.

Concept check

In a uniform electric field β particles are deflected much more than α particles of similar kinetic energy. This is mainly because β particles

B. The force on a β (charge e) is half that on an α (charge 2e), so A and C are wrong; what makes the difference is the mass, about 7200 times smaller, giving a far larger acceleration. D is wrong twice: β is faster, and a faster particle spends less time in the field, which would reduce the deflection.

Concept check

Which of the following statements about β and γ radiation is correct?

C: both are ionizing and both blacken film. A: γ ionizes too, weakly. B: both cross a vacuum (nothing is needed to carry either). D: γ has no charge, which is exactly why fields do not deflect it.

Concept check

A collimated beam from a source enters a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. Beyond the field a GM tube on the original line of the beam reads 95 counts per minute; a second GM tube placed below the line reads 520 counts per minute. Which deduction must be correct?

B. For a beam moving to the right in a field into the page, Fleming's rule sends a positive charge upwards and a negative charge downwards; a large count below the line must be β. A: 95 on the line could be γ, or could be entirely background, so γ is not proved. C: no tube was placed above the line, and α would in any case be absorbed by the air before arriving, so nothing can be said about α. D: 95 is an upper limit on the background (it may include some γ), not its value.

Concept check

A GM tube on the straight-through line from a source reads 184 counts per minute with no field and 82 counts per minute when a strong magnetic field is switched on across the beam. A tube far from the source reads 42 counts per minute. Estimate the β and γ count rates reaching the tube on the line, assuming any α is absorbed by the air.

The field removes the β from the line and leaves the γ and background: β ≈ 184 − 82 = 102. The far tube reads background only, so γ ≈ 82 − 42 = 40. Answer A. The other options forget to subtract either the field-on reading or the background.

Chapter 25

Summary: Radiation and Radioactivity

The whole chapter on one page: the facts to know cold, the equations to write, the traps examiners set, and the classified HKDSE questions for this chapter.

Learning objectives

Students should be able to:

  • realise X-rays as ionizing electromagnetic radiations of short wavelengths with high penetrating power

    2022/31 MC

  • realise the emission of X-rays when fast electrons hit a heavy metal target

    2022/31 MC

  • discuss the uses of X-rays

    2022/31 MC

  • describe the origin and nature of α, β and γ radiations

    2015/31 MC2017/32 MCPP/34 MC2016/32 MC2017/10 LQ2014/10 LQ

  • compare α, β and γ radiations in terms of their penetrating power, ranges, ionizing power, behaviour in electric field and magnetic field, and cloud chamber tracks

    2014/32 MC2016/32 MC2017/31 MC2017/32 MC2019/31 MCPP/34 MCPP/35 MCSAP/36 MC2014/10 LQ

  • realise the occurrence of radioactive decay in unstable nuclides

    2015/31 MC

  • realise the existence of background radiation

    2021/33 MC2020/30 MC

    2017/32 MC2014/32 MC2015/32 MCPP/35 MCSAP/36 MC

  • detect radiation in terms of count rate using a GM counter

    2014/32 MC2019/31 MC2020/30 MCPP/35 MCSAP/36 MC

  • suggest safety precautions in handling radioactive sources

    2015/32 MC2014/10 LQ

    2012/36 MC2013/34 MC2021/31 MC

  • use symbolic notations to represent nuclides

    2013/34 MC2014/31 MC2020/31 MC2021/31 MC2025/32 MC2026/12 LQ

  • define isotope

    2012/36 MC2014/31 MC2020/31 MC

    2021/33 MC

  • represent radioactive transmutations in α, β and γ decays using equations

    2013/34 MC2014/31 MC2020/31 MC2021/31 MC2025/32 MC2016/9 LQ2017/10 LQ2018/10 LQ2021/9 LQ2023/9 LQ2026/12 LQ

1Two pictures to keep

2α, β and γ at a glance

αβγ
Naturehelium nucleus, \( {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \)fast electron, \( {}^{0}_{-1}e \)very high-frequency EM wave
Originejected from the nucleusa neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton and an electronan excited nucleus loses energy, usually after α or β

3Notation and equations

\[ {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}: \quad A = Z + N, \quad N = A - Z \]
\[ {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \rightarrow {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\mathrm{Y} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He} \quad (\alpha) \]
\[ {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Y} + {}^{0}_{-1}e \quad (\beta) \]
\[ {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}^{*} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X} + \gamma \quad (\gamma) \]
\[ 4n_{\alpha} = \Delta A, \qquad 2n_{\alpha} - n_{\beta} = \Delta Z \]
\[ \text{corrected count rate} = \text{recorded} - \text{background} \]
  • Balance top and bottom separately: total \( A \) and total \( Z \) are the same on both sides. Emitted particles go on the right.
  • Every member of a decay series has \( A \) differing from the parent's by a multiple of 4; the end product is the lead isotope that satisfies this.
  • Isotopes: same \( Z \), different \( A \) (different \( N \)). Same chemistry, different mass. Not "same \( A \)".

4Detectors compared

DetectorWhat it showsDetects α?Tells the types apart on its own?
Photographic film / film badgeBlackening proportional to total dose over the exposure period; absorber windows on a badge hint at the typeNo: the light-proof wrapper stops αOnly roughly, via the absorber regions
GM counterCount rate (counts per second or minute), fast and precise; always includes background; never reads zeroYes, with the grid removed and the source within about 1.5 cmNo: needs absorbers or a field
Cloud chamberVisible tracks (droplets on the ions); random appearance shows decay is randomYes: thick straight tracksYes, from the track shape
Ionization current / spark counter / charged electroscopeAir made conducting by ion-pairs; current, sparks or dischargeYes (α is the strongest ionizer)No

5Traps that cost marks

A drop at 5 mm Al is not "β only"

Aluminium stops α as well as β. You need the paper step to rule out α and the lead step (a reading at background) to rule out γ.

Lead halves γ; it never zeroes it

Each 25 mm of lead halves the γ. A reading can never fall below background, and a reading that keeps changing with thickness is not background.

β bends more because of mass, not force

The force on an α is twice as large. The β is deflected more because it is about 7200 times lighter.

The β electron comes from the nucleus

A neutron becomes a proton and an electron. It is not an orbital electron, and no neutron is emitted.

Ions do the work, not the α

A charged object near an α source is neutralised by ions of the opposite sign drawn out of the ionized air. Moving the source a few centimetres away ends the effect.

X-rays are not nuclear radiation

Undeflected radiation from a radioactive source is γ. X-rays and γ differ only in origin; both are ionizing EM waves.

Irradiated is not contaminated

An X-rayed patient or a wrapped film under a source has absorbed energy and is not radioactive. Only radioactive material on or in an object makes it radioactive.

"α particle", not "α decay"

When asked to state the kind of radiation, name the particle. A radium source also gives β and γ because its daughters are radioactive, not because it is impure.

Concept check

A source emitting α, β and γ radiation is placed in a vacuum in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. Three paths are seen: P curves slightly one way, Q is straight, R curves sharply the other way. Which identification is correct?

The undeflected path must be the uncharged γ, so Q = γ (A, C, D all give Q a charged particle). Of the two charged radiations the light β curves sharply, so R = β and P = α: B. The two curves are on opposite sides because the charges have opposite signs.

Concept check

A nuclide P decays by α emission to Q, and Q decays by β emission to R. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. P and R have the same number of neutrons.
  2. R has one more proton than Q.
  3. The mass numbers of Q and R are equal.

Let P be \( (Z, N) \). Q = \( (Z-2, N-2) \); R = \( (Z-1, N-3) \). (1) is false: R has three fewer neutrons than P. (2) is true: β adds a proton. (3) is true: β leaves \( A \) unchanged. Answer C.

Concept check

Which of the following would reduce the count rate registered by a GM tube placed 10 cm from a β source in air?

  1. inserting a 5 mm aluminium sheet between source and tube
  2. applying a strong magnetic field across the path
  3. inserting a sheet of paper between source and tube

(1) stops the β. (2) deflects the β off the line to the tube, so fewer arrive. (3) does nothing measurable: paper stops α, and β passes through it. Answer D. (Reversing the polarity of deflecting plates would also do it; distance already exceeds the α range, so α plays no part.)
