Book 5 · Ch.226.1 Rate of radioactive decay
Map 26.1 26.2 26.3 Summary

26.1

Rate of radioactive decay

Decay is random for one nucleus and perfectly predictable for a large sample. This section builds the two working tools, half-life and activity, shows how to read them from real (background-contaminated) data, and then, as extension, the decay constant and the exponential law that let you solve for any time, not only whole half-lives.

Learning objectives

Students should be able to:

  • examine the random nature of radioactive decay

    2020/30 MC

  • state the proportional relationship between the activity of a sample and the number of undecayed nuclei

    SAP/35 MC2025/31 MC2023/31 MC

  • define half-life as the period of time over which the number of radioactive nuclei decreases by a factor of one-half

    2023/31 MC2012/35 MC

  • determine the half-life of a radioisotope from its decay graph or from numerical data

    2012/35 MC2013/35 MC2016/33 MC2018/32 MC2020/33 MC2022/32 MC2024/32 MC2013/9 LQ2016/9 LQ2018/10 LQ2023/9 LQ2025/12 LQ

  • realise the existence of background radiation

    2020/30 MC

  • solve problems involving radioactive decay

    2012/35 MC2013/35 MC2016/33 MC2018/32 MC2019/32 MC2020/33 MC2021/32 MC2022/32 MC2023/31 MC2024/32 MC2015/33 MC2013/9 LQ2016/9 LQ2018/10 LQ2021/9 LQ2023/9 LQ2025/12 LQ

  • represent the number of undecayed nuclei by the exponential law of decay \( N = N_0 e^{-kt} \) extension

    2020/32 MC2019/32 MC2013/9 LQ2025/12 LQ

  • apply the exponential law of decay \( N = N_0 e^{-kt} \) to solve problems extension

    2020/32 MC2019/32 MC2013/9 LQ2025/12 LQ

  • relate the decay constant and the half-life extension

    2020/32 MC2019/32 MC2013/9 LQ2025/12 LQ

ADecay is random, but a sample is predictable

Random and spontaneous

Radioactive decay is random: it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, and every undecayed nucleus of a given nuclide has the same chance of decaying in the next second, however old it is. It is spontaneous: it happens on its own and nothing external (temperature, pressure, chemical bonding, an electric field) speeds it up or slows it down.

  • Because every nucleus has the same chance per unit time, the number decaying per second is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present. Fewer survivors, fewer decays. That is why the rate falls as the sample decays.
  • With a large number of nuclei (a microgram of anything contains about \( 10^{15} \) atoms) the statistical average is so reliable that the decay of a sample follows a smooth, predictable curve.
  • With very few nuclei the average is not reliable. If a million boxes each hold two nuclei and you wait one half-life, some boxes will have 0 left, some 1, some 2; only the average is 1. "Half of two nuclei decays after one half-life" is not a meaningful statement.
  • Evidence of randomness: repeated equal-time counts of the same source (or of background) are never identical, and cloud-chamber tracks appear at random places and moments.

Concept check

Radioactive decay is described as random. This means that

D is the definition. A is true but is a consequence of every nucleus having the same chance, not what "random" means. B is false: decay is spontaneous and temperature has no effect. C is false: a given nuclide always emits the same radiation; what is unknown is the timing.

Concept check

Four one-minute background counts are taken in the same laboratory. Which set of readings is the most probable?

Background is roughly constant on average but random in detail, so consecutive counts should scatter a little about a mean: D. B shows no randomness at all; A swings far too wildly for a steady source; C falls steadily, which would mean a decaying source, not background.

Concept check

A sample contains a very large number of nuclei of one radionuclide. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. The nuclei that have survived longest are the most likely to decay next.
  2. The number decaying per second falls as time goes on.
  3. Cooling the sample would slow its decay.

(1) is false: nuclei do not age; every survivor has the same chance per second. (2) is true: fewer undecayed nuclei remain, so fewer decay per second. (3) is false: decay is spontaneous and unaffected by temperature. Answer C.

BHalf-life

Definition

The half-life \( T_{1/2} \) of a radionuclide is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to fall to half its initial value. Equivalently, it is the time for the activity to fall to half. After \( n \) half-lives,

\[ N = N_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}, \qquad n = \frac{t}{T_{1/2}} \]
  • Half-life is a property of the nuclide, not of the sample. A gram and a microgram of iodine-131 both have \( T_{1/2} = 8 \) d. Heating, cooling, dissolving or splitting the sample does not change it.
  • Half-life is not "how long the source lasts". After one half-life half the nuclei are still undecayed; after two, a quarter; the number approaches zero but a sample is never "finished" at any particular moment.
  • The decayed nuclei do not disappear. They become the daughter nuclide, so the total number of nuclei (and, very nearly, the mass) stays constant while the sample becomes progressively more daughter and less parent.
  • Half-lives range over more than twenty powers of ten:
RadionuclideHalf-lifeRadionuclideHalf-life
polonium-2150.0018 siodine-1318 d
radon-22052 sstrontium-9028.8 y
bismuth-21345.6 mincarbon-145730 y (often rounded to 5700 y)
sodium-2415 huranium-238\( 4.47 \times 10^{9} \) y
Worked example

A sample of a radionuclide with half-life 3 days has mass 100 g. (a) What mass of the nuclide remains after 12 days? (b) What mass has decayed? (c) What was the mass 6 days before the start?

  1. (a) \( n = 12/3 = 4 \) half-lives. Remaining \( = 100 \times (1/2)^4 = 6.25 \) g.
  2. (b) Decayed \( = 100 - 6.25 = 93.75 \) g. (It is still in the sample, as daughter nuclide.)
  3. (c) Going backwards two half-lives doubles twice: \( 100 \times 2^2 = 400 \) g.

Common slips: giving 6.25 g for "decayed", or 75 g (two half-lives) for "decayed in 12 days".

Concept check

Which of the following statements about the half-life of a radioactive source is/are correct?

  1. It is the time for the activity of the source to fall to half its value.
  2. It is the time the source remains radioactive.
  3. It is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei to fall to half its value.

(3) is the definition and (1) follows because \( A \propto N \). (2) is the standard misconception: after one half-life the source is still radioactive with half its nuclei left. Answer B.

Concept check

A source contains only radioactive nuclide X, which decays to stable Y. After one half-life of X, which of the following is/are correct?

  1. The number of X nuclei is about half the initial number.
  2. The number of Y nuclei is about twice its initial value.
  3. The activity of the source is about half its initial value.

(1) and (3) are the definition of half-life applied to \( N \) and \( A \). (2) is a trap: the source started with no Y, so there is no "initial value" to double. After one half-life the Y nuclei equal the X nuclei. Answer C.

Concept check

A pure sample of a radionuclide decays to a stable daughter. After 2 years the sample is 2% parent and 98% daughter by number. What was its composition after 1 year?

Whatever fraction survives one year, the same fraction of that survives the next year. So \( f^2 = 0.02 \), \( f = \sqrt{0.02} = 0.14 \): C. A assumes the fraction falls linearly; B assumes half of the loss happens each year; D doubles instead of taking the square root.

CActivity

Definition

The activity \( A \) of a sample is the number of nuclei that decay per unit time. Unit: the becquerel (Bq), 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. Because every undecayed nucleus has the same chance of decaying per second, activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei:

\[ A \propto N \qquad\text{so}\qquad A = A_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n} \]
  • Activity depends on two things: how many undecayed nuclei there are, and the nuclide's half-life (a short half-life means each nucleus is more likely to decay per second). It does not depend on the type of radiation emitted.
  • Halving a sample halves \( N \) and therefore \( A \). It leaves the half-life unchanged.
  • Count rate is not activity. A GM tube some distance away records far fewer counts per second than the activity in Bq: radiation is emitted in all directions and the tube intercepts only a small fraction; some is absorbed on the way; the tube does not register every particle that enters it. The corrected count rate is proportional to activity, so it halves on the same clock and can be used to find the half-life.
  • Non-integer numbers of half-lives are allowed: \( n = t / T_{1/2} \) need not be a whole number. \( A = A_0 (1/2)^{t/T_{1/2}} \) works for any \( t \).
Worked example

Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample has activity 200 Bq after 30 days. What was its initial activity?

  1. \( n = 30/8 = 3.75 \) half-lives (do not round to 3 or 4).
  2. \( A_0 = A \times 2^{n} = 200 \times 2^{3.75} = 200 \times 13.45 = 2690 \) Bq.

Rounding \( n \) to 4 gives 3200 Bq; to 3 gives 1600 Bq; multiplying by 3.75 gives 750 Bq. All three appear as distractors.

Concept check

A source undergoes decay such that 300 nuclei decay in 1 minute. Its activity is

Activity is decays per second: \( 300 / 60 = 5 \) Bq, B. C forgets the unit conversion; D multiplies instead of dividing; A inverts.

Concept check

Half of a powdered radioactive sample is removed. For the half that remains, which of the following are halved compared with the original sample?

  1. the activity
  2. the half-life
  3. the number of undecayed nuclei

Half the powder means half the nuclei (3), and since \( A \propto N \) half the activity (1). The half-life is a property of the nuclide and is unchanged. Answer A.

Concept check

On which of the following does the activity of a radioactive source depend?

  1. the nature of the radiation emitted
  2. the half-life of the nuclide
  3. the number of undecayed nuclei

\( A = kN \): the number of nuclei (3) and, through \( k = \ln 2 / T_{1/2} \), the half-life (2). Whether the decay gives α, β or γ has no bearing on how many decays occur per second. Answer D.

Concept check

Two samples P and Q are of the same radionuclide. P has twice as many undecayed nuclei as Q. Which of the following is correct?

C: \( A \propto N \) gives the factor of two; half-life is fixed by the nuclide, so both halve on the same clock. A and D make the half-life depend on the amount; B ignores \( N \).

DReading half-life from real data

Corrected count rate

Background radiation (cosmic rays, rocks and soil, building materials, food and drink, radon in the air) gives a GM tube a small, roughly steady count rate even with no source nearby. The corrected count rate is the recorded count rate minus the background count rate, and it is the quantity proportional to the activity of the source.

\[ \text{corrected count rate} = \text{recorded count rate} - \text{background count rate} \]
Worked example

In Example 26.1 the recorded count rate starts at 840 min-1 and flattens at about 40 min-1. Find the half-life.

  1. Background \( \approx 40 \) min-1 (the level the graph flattens to). Corrected initial rate \( = 840 - 40 = 800 \) min-1.
  2. After one half-life the corrected rate is 400 min-1, so the recorded rate is \( 400 + 40 = 440 \) min-1.
  3. Read the time at which the recorded curve passes 440 min-1: 10 h. So \( T_{1/2} = 10 \) h.

Reading the time to fall from 840 to 420 on the uncorrected curve gives a half-life that is too long. Always halve the corrected value, then add background back before reading the graph.

  • Why the curve flattens. The corrected count rate approaches zero but never quite reaches it (each half-life only halves what is left). Long before that, the source's contribution has fallen below the background, so the recorded rate levels off at the background value.
  • From a table. Subtract background from every reading, then find the half-life from the corrected column (or plot it and read the graph). A single corrected reading can come out slightly negative or below background because both source and background counts fluctuate randomly; treat it as "about zero".
  • Each reading more than half the previous in equal time steps does not mean a long half-life; it is the signature of an uncorrected background. Subtract it and check again.
  • Scatter. Points that do not lie exactly on a smooth curve are expected: decay is random. Draw the best smooth curve through them.
  • A second run with a weaker source of the same nuclide starts lower but has the same half-life and flattens at the same background level.
  • Reduce background error by counting for longer and by measuring background for a long time before and after the experiment.
Worked example

A GM counter near a source reads 1000 min-1. Two half-lives later it reads 400 min-1. (a) Find the background count rate. (b) What will it read after a further half-life?

  1. (a) Let background be \( b \). Corrected start \( = 1000 - b \). After two half-lives corrected \( = (1000 - b)/4 \), so recorded \( = (1000 - b)/4 + b = 400 \). Then \( 1000 - b + 4b = 1600 \), \( b = 200 \) min-1.
  2. (b) Corrected after three half-lives \( = 800/8 = 100 \); recorded \( = 100 + 200 = 300 \) min-1.

Dividing 1000 by 4 and comparing with 400 "proves" nothing: the mismatch is the background.

Concept check

It takes 2.0 years for the activity of a sample to drop from 800 Bq to 600 Bq. How long will it take to drop from 600 Bq to 300 Bq?

Falling to 3/4 took 2.0 y. Falling to 1/2 is a bigger drop, so it takes longer than 2.0 y; and 3/4 squared is 9/16, still more than 1/2, so two such periods (4.0 y) are not enough either: the answer must exceed 4.0 y, leaving D. Exactly: \( (3/4)^{T/2} = 1/2 \) gives \( T = 2 \ln(1/2)/\ln(3/4) = 4.8 \) y. A treats equal drops in Bq as taking equal times; decay is not linear.

Concept check

A GM counter records 140 min-1 when a source is first placed near it. After a long time the reading settles at 20 min-1. At what recorded count rate should you read the graph to find one half-life?

Corrected start \( = 140 - 20 = 120 \); half of that is 60; recorded \( = 60 + 20 = 80 \) min-1, B. A halves the uncorrected reading; C forgets to add the background back before reading the recorded curve; D halves the background.

Concept check

Counts per minute from a source are recorded every minute, with background about 100 min-1: 900, 417, 225, 150, 113, 92, 102. Which explanation of the reading of 92 is best?

By 5 minutes the corrected rate is close to zero, so the reading is essentially background, and background counts vary randomly from minute to minute: B. Activity cannot be negative (A); half-life is constant (C); a slightly low count is normal, not a fault (D). From the first three corrected values, 800, 317, 125, each minute multiplies by about 0.4, giving \( T_{1/2} \approx 45 \) s.

EComparing two sources

A longer half-life does not mean a weaker source, and a stronger source now does not mean a longer-lasting one. Both the starting activity and the half-life matter. Amy and Bob each buy a device that stops working when the source's activity falls below 1000 Bq:

Initial activityHalf-lifeActivity year by yearWorking life
Amy8000 Bq2 y8000 → 4000 (2 y) → 2000 (4 y) → 1000 (6 y)about 6 y
Bob16 000 Bq1 y16 000 → 8000 (1 y) → 4000 (2 y) → 2000 (3 y) → 1000 (4 y)about 4 y
  • Bob's source starts stronger but dies first: four halvings in 4 years against Amy's three in 6 years.
  • For equal numbers of nuclei, the shorter half-life gives the higher activity (each nucleus is more likely to decay per second). For unequal amounts you must compare \( A = kN \) directly.
  • On a graph of activity against time, the curve that falls more steeply as a fraction of its current value has the shorter half-life. Two curves that cross have equal activity at that moment, but the one with the shorter half-life has fewer undecayed nuclei there (\( N = A/k \) with larger \( k \)).

Concept check

Half-lives: carbon-11 20.3 min; phosphorus-32 14.3 d; sodium-22 2.60 y. Which of the following is/are correct?

  1. The activity of a carbon-11 sample must be the highest of the three.
  2. The decay constant of phosphorus-32 is larger than that of carbon-11.
  3. If a sodium-22 sample starts at 1520 Bq, after 6 years its activity is lower than 380 Bq.

(1) false: activity also depends on the number of nuclei, which is not given. (2) false: the shorter half-life (C-11) has the larger decay constant. (3) true: 6 y is more than two half-lives (5.2 y), so the activity is below \( 1520/4 = 380 \) Bq. Answer B.

Concept check

A radionuclide has a half-life of 20 hours. After 10 hours the fraction \( f \) of the original nuclei remaining satisfies

Half a half-life. The fraction is more than 1/2 (only a full half-life gets you to 1/2), but less than 3/4, because more decays happen in the first half of the period (more nuclei present) than in the second: \( f = (1/2)^{0.5} = 0.71 \). C. D is the linear-decay error ("half the time, half the loss").

Concept check

Initially a sample contains 4 times as many nuclei of X (half-life \( t \)) as of Y (half-life \( 2t \)). After how long are the numbers of X and Y nuclei equal?

Set \( 4N(1/2)^{T/t} = N(1/2)^{T/2t} \). Writing 4 as \( 2^2 \): \( 2 - T/t = -T/2t \), so \( T/2t = 2 \), \( T = 4t \): D. Check: after \( 4t \), X has had 4 half-lives (factor 1/16, so \( 4N/16 = N/4 \)) and Y has had 2 (factor 1/4, so \( N/4 \)).

FThe decay constant and the exponential law extension

Definition

The decay constant \( k \) of a nuclide is the probability that any one undecayed nucleus decays per unit time; equivalently, the fraction of the undecayed nuclei that decay per unit time. Unit: s-1 (or min-1, h-1, y-1). If \( k = 0.2 \) s-1, each nucleus has a 1-in-5 chance of decaying in the next second, so about one fifth of the undecayed nuclei decay each second.

\[ A = kN \]
\[ N = N_0 e^{-kt}, \qquad A = A_0 e^{-kt} \]
\[ k = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} \]
\[ t = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{N_0}{N} = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{A_0}{A} \]
  • \( k \) is not the activity. Activity is decays per second for the whole sample and falls with time; \( k \) is per nucleus and is constant for a given nuclide. Like the half-life, \( k \) identifies the nuclide and is unchanged by temperature, pressure, chemical state or the amount of sample.
  • Large \( k \) means short half-life: \( k T_{1/2} = \ln 2 \) always. Both describe the same thing.
  • The decay law follows from \( A = kN \): the rate of loss of \( N \) is proportional to \( N \), and the only function that does that is the exponential. \( (1/2)^{t/T_{1/2}} \) and \( e^{-kt} \) are the same curve written two ways.
  • On a graph of \( \ln A \) (or \( \ln N \)) against \( t \), the points lie on a straight line: \( \ln A = \ln A_0 - kt \). Slope \( = -k \), intercept \( = \ln A_0 \). A mixture of two nuclides gives a curve that is straight only at the ends (the short-lived one dominates early, the long-lived one late).
  • The probability that a given nucleus decays within time \( t \) is \( 1 - e^{-kt} \), not \( kt \) (that approximation only works when \( kt \ll 1 \)).
  • Units. Keep \( k \) and \( t \) in the same unit. Convert \( k \) to s-1 before using \( A = kN \) with \( A \) in Bq.
  • Counting nuclei from mass. \( N = \dfrac{m}{M} \times N_A \), where \( M \) is the molar mass in grams (numerically the mass number) and \( N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \) mol-1; or \( N = m / (\text{mass of one atom}) \). Watch the mass units: 1 μg \( = 10^{-6} \) g.
Worked example

The number of undecayed nuclei in a sample falls to one third of its initial value in 50 days. (a) Find the decay constant. (b) How long does it take to fall to one tenth? (c) How long does it take to fall by one third?

  1. (a) \( N/N_0 = 1/3 = e^{-k(50)} \). Taking ln: \( \ln 3 = 50k \), \( k = 1.099/50 = 0.0220 \) d-1.
  2. (b) \( 1/10 = e^{-kt} \), \( t = \ln 10 / k = 2.303/0.0220 = 105 \) d.
  3. (c) Falling by one third leaves \( N/N_0 = 2/3 \). \( t = \ln(3/2)/k = 0.405/0.0220 = 18.5 \) d.

"Decreases by one third" and "decreases to one third" are different questions. Read the stem twice.

Worked example

A 1 μg sample of plutonium-239 has activity 2300 Bq. Find (a) the number of Pu-239 nuclei, (b) the decay constant, (c) the half-life in years. (\( N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \) mol-1; 1 y \( = 3.15 \times 10^{7} \) s.)

  1. (a) \( N_0 = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-6}}{239} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 2.52 \times 10^{15} \).
  2. (b) \( k = A/N = 2300 / (2.52 \times 10^{15}) = 9.13 \times 10^{-13} \) s-1.
  3. (c) \( T_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k = 7.59 \times 10^{11} \) s \( = 7.59 \times 10^{11} / (3.15 \times 10^{7}) = 24\,100 \) y.

Concept check

Which statement about the decay constant of a radionuclide is incorrect?

A describes the activity, which depends on how much sample there is and falls with time. B and C are two wordings of the definition of \( k \); D is true because decay is spontaneous.

Concept check

A radionuclide has decay constant \( 1.02 \times 10^{-5} \) s-1. The time for the number of undecayed nuclei to decrease by one third is about

Decreasing by one third leaves 2/3: \( t = \ln(3/2)/k = 0.405/(1.02 \times 10^{-5}) = 3.98 \times 10^{4} \) s, B. A is the time to fall to one third (\( \ln 3 / k \)); C is one half-life; D uses \( kt = 1/3 \), the linear approximation.

Concept check

For a certain source, a graph of \( \ln A \) against \( t \) is a straight line through \( (0, 6.0) \) and \( (4.0 \text{ h}, 2.0) \). Which of the following is correct?

\( \ln A = \ln A_0 - kt \). Slope \( = (2.0 - 6.0)/4.0 = -1.0 \) h-1, so \( k = 1.0 \) h-1 and \( T_{1/2} = 0.693/1.0 = 0.69 \) h: C. The intercept is \( \ln A_0 = 6.0 \), so \( A_0 = e^{6} \approx 400 \) Bq, not 6 Bq (D).

Concept check

A nuclide has decay constant \( 0.05 \) s-1. The probability that a particular undecayed nucleus decays within the next 10 s is

The probability of surviving 10 s is \( e^{-kt} = e^{-0.5} = 0.61 \) (C is the survival probability). So the probability of decaying is \( 1 - 0.61 = 0.39 \), B. A is \( kt \), which overestimates because the chance is applied to a shrinking population; D is the probability per second.

Write it out

A 0.040 mg sample of iron-60 (molar mass 59.9 g) has an activity of 3400 Bq. (a) Find the number of iron-60 nuclei. (b) Find the decay constant. (c) Find the half-life in seconds, and comment on why iron-60 is found in samples of lunar soil that formed millions of years ago. (\( N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \) mol-1.) (5 marks)

  1. (a) \( N = \dfrac{0.040 \times 10^{-3}}{59.9} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 4.02 \times 10^{17} \).
  2. (b) \( k = A/N = 3400 / (4.02 \times 10^{17}) = 8.46 \times 10^{-15} \) s-1.
  3. (c) \( T_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k = 0.693 / (8.46 \times 10^{-15}) = 8.2 \times 10^{13} \) s (about 2.6 million years).
  4. A half-life of millions of years means only a small fraction of any iron-60 present when the soil formed has decayed, so measurable amounts remain.

Mass conversion (1), \( N \) (1), \( k \) (1), \( T_{1/2} \) (1), comment linking long half-life to survival (1).

Map 26.1 26.2 26.3 Summary

26.2

Uses of radionuclides

Every use of a radionuclide is a choice of radiation type and half-life, and sometimes of chemistry, to fit a job. Exam questions almost never ask "which isotope"; they ask "why this one and not that one". This section gives the reasons in the form the mark scheme wants.

Learning objectives

Students should be able to:

  • discuss uses of radioactive isotopes

    2024/33 MC2015/33 MC2014/10 LQ2017/10 LQ2018/10 LQ2021/9 LQ2026/12 LQ

  • realise the existence of radioactive isotopes in some elements

    2021/33 MC

  • determine the half-life of a radioisotope from its decay graph or from numerical data

    2015/33 MC2013/9 LQ2025/12 LQ

  • solve problems involving radioactive decay

    2015/33 MC2013/9 LQ2025/12 LQ

AChoosing a radionuclide for a job

Three questions decide the choice. Which radiation? It must get from the source to where it is detected or where it must act, and no further. How long a half-life? Long enough for the job to be finished, short enough not to linger where it is unwanted; for instruments, long enough that the activity stays steady for years. What chemistry? Anything put into a body or a plant must go where the element normally goes and must not be poisonous, and neither must its daughter.

UseRadiation, and whyHalf-life, and why
Medical tracer (imaging)γ: penetrates out of the body to an external detector; weakly ionizing so does little damage insideHours to days (Tc-99m 6 h, I-131 8 d): long enough to take the images, short enough to limit the dose after
Internal radiotherapyβ: absorbed within a few millimetres, so the dose stays in the target tissue; ionizes less severely than αDays to weeks (I-131 8 d, Sr-89 about 50 d): long enough to complete the treatment, short enough to avoid long-term exposure
External radiotherapyγ: penetrates deep into the body to reach the tumourYears (Co-60 5.27 y): the source need not be replaced often
Leak in a buried pipeγ: passes through soil to a detector at the surfaceHours (Na-24 15 h): long enough to complete the survey, short enough that contamination of soil and water fades in days
Thickness gauge, level monitorβ for paper, plastic, foil; γ for steel or lead. The radiation must be partly absorbed, so the count changes with thickness. α is stopped completelyYears: the count rate stays steady, so the gauge does not need frequent recalibration or replacement
Smoke detectorα: strongly ionizing (a steady ion current in air); very short range so nothing escapes the chamberHundreds of years (Am-241 432 y): a stable ionization level for the life of the device
Plant nutrient tracerβ (P-32): detectable through leaf tissue with a GM tube; the element follows ordinary phosphorus14.3 d: long enough for the plant to transport it and for the survey; P-34 (12 s) would decay before it moved
Food irradiation, sterilizing equipmentγ (Co-60), or X-rays: penetrates packaging and the whole item, killing microbes by damaging their cells. α cannot get inYears: a steady, long-lived source in a shielded room
Carbon-14 datingβ, but the radiation is not chosen; the constant half-life is the clock5730 y: dates once-living material from about 60 y to 60 000 y
Exam tip

When a table of candidate isotopes is given, eliminate by radiation type first, then by half-life, and give the reason for each rejection. "α cannot leave the body" or "a 45-minute half-life would decay before the survey ends" earns the mark; naming the right letter alone does not.

Concept check

A radionuclide to be injected into a patient as a tracer should have

  1. a non-toxic parent and a non-toxic daughter
  2. high ionizing power
  3. high penetrating power

(3): the radiation must be detected outside the body. (1): the tracer stays in the body, and so does whatever it decays into. (2) is the opposite of what is wanted: ionization inside the body is damage. Answer B.

BMedical uses

Tracers

  • A γ-emitting nuclide is attached to a compound the body sends to the organ of interest: iodine to the thyroid, sodium into the blood, technetium-99m compounds to bone or brain. A γ camera outside the body maps where the activity gathers. Only a tiny amount is injected, so the activity, and the dose, is small.
  • α is never used as a tracer for two separate reasons: it cannot be detected outside the body (range in tissue is a fraction of a millimetre) and it ionizes strongly, so it would damage cells. A nuclide emitting α or β along with γ is also unsuitable for the same reason.
  • Half-life, two-sided: long enough to prepare the dose and take the images, short enough that the activity in the patient falls to a safe level within days. Too long a half-life keeps the activity high inside the body for weeks.
  • Assumption in tracer calculations: none of the tracer is lost from the body (excreted) during the measurement. If some is excreted, the measured concentration is lower than it should be, so a calculated blood volume comes out too large.
Worked example

A doctor injects 20 000 Bq of sodium-24 (half-life 15 h) into a patient's bloodstream. 45 hours later a 10 cm3 blood sample has an activity of 5 Bq. Estimate the patient's blood volume, stating one assumption.

  1. 45 h is 3 half-lives, so the total activity remaining in the blood is \( 20\,000 / 8 = 2500 \) Bq.
  2. The tracer is spread evenly: 5 Bq in every 10 cm3, so \( V = 10 \times \dfrac{2500}{5} = 5000 \) cm3.
  3. Assumptions: the tracer is uniformly mixed through the blood, and none has been excreted.

Forgetting the decay (using 20 000 Bq) gives 40 000 cm3, which is not a human blood volume. Always decay the injected activity to the time of sampling first.

Internal radiotherapy

  • A β emitter is taken up by the target tissue (iodine-131 by the thyroid, strontium-89 by bone). β is chosen because it travels only a few millimetres in tissue, so the energy is deposited in the tumour and not in other organs (γ would pass right through), and because it ionizes less intensely than α, avoiding severe local damage.
  • Half-life of days to weeks: long enough to deliver the treatment, short enough that the patient does not carry significant activity for months.
  • Many β emitters, including I-131, also give γ, which leaves the body. Patients are isolated for a few days after treatment, and airport radiation detectors have picked up treated patients weeks later.

External radiotherapy

  • γ is used because it penetrates the skull and tissue to reach a deep tumour. α and β would be absorbed in the skin and bone.
  • Cobalt-60 (half-life 5.27 y) is replaced every few years. The sources decay whether or not the machine is in use, so halving the machine's daily use does not let the sources last longer.

Write it out

Give two different reasons why an α-emitting radionuclide is never used as a medical tracer, and explain why the half-life of a tracer should be neither too short nor too long. (4 marks)

  1. α particles have a range of a fraction of a millimetre in tissue, so they cannot be detected outside the body.
  2. α is strongly ionizing, so it would cause severe damage to cells near where it collects.
  3. Too short: the activity would fall too low to detect before the images are taken.
  4. Too long: the patient would carry a significant activity, and receive a dose, for a long time after the examination.

Concept check

A hospital's cobalt-60 radiotherapy sources are replaced every five years. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. Using the machine for fewer hours each day would let the sources last longer.
  2. The sources are replaced because their activity, not their penetrating power, has fallen.
  3. Cobalt-60 is used because γ radiation can reach a tumour deep inside the body.

(1) is false: nuclei decay at the same rate whether the shutter is open or closed. (2) is true: each γ photon is as penetrating as ever; there are simply fewer per second, so treatments would take too long. (3) is the reason for choosing γ. Answer C.

Concept check

Which radionuclide is most suitable for external diagnostic imaging of the brain?

Imaging from outside needs γ, which rules out A and D however convenient their half-lives. Of the two γ emitters, 13.5 years (B) would leave the patient radioactive for decades; 6 hours (C, technetium-99m) is long enough to image and gone within a couple of days.

CIndustrial uses: tracers and gauges

Finding a leak in a buried pipe

  • γ because it must pass through a metre or so of soil to the detector. β would be stopped in the soil, α in the pipe wall.
  • Half-life of hours (sodium-24, 15 h): long enough to finish the survey, short enough that the soil and water are not left contaminated for long. Months would be far too long.

Thickness gauge

  • Feedback. If the sheet comes out too thin, more β gets through and the count rate rises; the control system moves the rollers closer together. Too thick, the count falls and the rollers open. The set point is the count rate for the correct thickness.
  • Which radiation. The radiation must be partly absorbed by the sheet, so that the count is sensitive to thickness. For paper, plastic film or aluminium foil that is β (α would be stopped completely, γ would pass almost unchanged). For thick steel plate or lead slabs β is stopped completely, so γ is the right choice.
  • Long half-life (years) so the count rate for the correct thickness stays the same; otherwise the gauge would need frequent recalibration and the source frequent replacement.
  • As the source ages its activity falls (fewer particles per second). The penetrating power of each β particle does not change with time.

Level monitor

The same idea checks whether cartons on a filling line are full. A β source and a detector face each other at the fill line. A full carton absorbs most of the β; an under-filled one lets it through and the count is abnormally high, so the carton is rejected. α could not pass through the carton at all, and γ would pass through the liquid almost unchanged. A source with a half-life of years is needed; ten minutes would be useless.

Concept check

A radioisotope is to be added to water in an underground pipe so that a leak can be located from above ground. Which is most suitable?

Only γ can reach a detector through soil, so B. A has a workable half-life but β is absorbed by the soil; C and D give α, which would not even leave the water. 36 h is long enough for the survey and short enough that the soil is not contaminated for long.

Concept check

Four sources are available for a gauge that monitors the thickness of lead slabs, about 2 cm thick, as they leave a rolling mill. Which is most suitable?

β (B) is the right choice for paper or foil, but 2 cm of lead stops every β particle, so the count would read zero whatever the thickness. γ is partly absorbed by lead (about half per 25 mm), so its count changes measurably with thickness: C. D is γ but would need recalibrating every hour. A is stopped by anything.

Concept check

Andrew says the β source in a paper-thickness gauge must be replaced after some years "because the penetrating power of the β particles falls with time". Which is the best comment?

B. The energy of the β particles from a given nuclide does not depend on the age of the source; what falls is how many are emitted per second. C ignores that even a long half-life eventually matters; D is false: β does not make the paper radioactive.

Write it out

Explain how a β source and a detector keep aluminium foil at the required thickness in a rolling mill, and state why a source with a long half-life is chosen. (4 marks)

  1. β from the source passes through the foil to the detector; the thicker the foil, the more β is absorbed and the lower the count rate.
  2. If the count rate rises above the set value, the foil is too thin and the rollers are moved closer together; if it falls below, the foil is too thick and the rollers are moved apart.
  3. A long half-life means the activity, and so the count rate for the correct thickness, stays practically constant for years.
  4. So the gauge does not need frequent recalibration or replacement of the source.

DSmoke detector

  • The current is carried by the ions the α particles make in the air, not by the α particles themselves. Smoke particles capture the ions, making heavy, slow carriers, so the current drops.
  • α is chosen because it is the strongest ionizer, giving a usable current from a very weak source, and because its range in air is only a few centimetres, so no radiation leaves the chamber. Occupants of the room receive no extra dose.
  • Half-life of hundreds of years (Am-241, 432 y) keeps the ionization level, and so the "clear air" current, stable for the life of the detector. A short half-life is not wanted here.
Worked example

A smoke detector fails when the activity of its Am-241 source (half-life 432 y) falls to 80% of its initial value. Will it still work after 100 years?

  1. \( k = \ln 2 / 432 = 1.60 \times 10^{-3} \) y-1.
  2. \( 0.80 = e^{-kt} \) gives \( t = \ln(1/0.80)/k = 0.223 / (1.60 \times 10^{-3}) = 139 \) y.
  3. 139 y is more than 100 y, so yes.

Concept check

Which of the following statements about an ionization smoke detector is/are correct?

  1. The current between the plates is carried by α particles crossing the gap.
  2. A source with a half-life of a few days would be a better choice because it would be less hazardous.
  3. People in the room receive no significant dose from the source because α has a range of a few centimetres in air.

(1) false: the α particles ionize the air and the ions carry the current. (2) false: the detector would stop working in weeks as the ion current fell; a long half-life keeps the current steady. (3) true. Answer D.

EIrradiation: food, medical equipment, pests

  • γ (or X-rays, which are equally ionizing and penetrating) because it must reach the whole of a sealed package. α could not penetrate the wrapping, let alone the food.
  • The same process sterilizes sealed syringes, dressings and surgical instruments, which cannot be heat-treated after packaging, and sterilizes insect pests so that a population dies out.
  • A steady source with a half-life of years (Co-60, 5.27 y) is used, in a shielded room with remote handling.
  • For or against: irradiated food keeps longer and carries fewer disease organisms; some people object that it may alter taste or nutrients, or distrust the label. Either is acceptable in an exam if supported by a reason.

Concept check

Which of the following statements about food irradiation is/are correct?

  1. An α source must be used, because α has the highest ionizing power.
  2. γ must not be used, because its high penetrating power would make the food radioactive.
  3. X-rays cannot be used, because they are not nuclear radiation.

(1): α cannot get through the packaging or into the food. (2): penetration is exactly why γ is used, and irradiating food does not make it radioactive. (3): X-rays are ionizing EM waves just like γ, and are used. Answer D.

FCarbon-14 dating

Isotopes of carbon

Natural carbon is about 99% carbon-12 and 1% carbon-13, both stable, with a trace (about one atom in \( 10^{12} \)) of radioactive carbon-14. C-14 is made continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic-ray neutrons strike nitrogen, \( {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{p} \), and it decays by β emission, \( {}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}e \). Production balances decay, so the C-14 fraction in atmospheric carbon dioxide stays roughly constant.

  • Why it works. Plants take in CO2 and animals eat plants, so every living thing has the atmospheric C-14 fraction and the same activity per gram of carbon. When it dies the intake stops and the C-14 decays without replacement. Comparing the activity per gram (or the C-14 : C-12 ratio) of the sample with that of living material gives the number of half-lives since death.
  • Assumptions. The atmospheric C-14 fraction was the same when the organism lived as it is today, and the organism had that fraction at death. (Burning fossil fuels adds C-12, diluting the fraction; nuclear tests added C-14, enriching it. Both need corrections.)
  • What cannot be dated. Anything living (the fraction is still being topped up, so the clock has not started). Rocks, metals and pottery (never had a living carbon fraction). Fossil fuels: millions of years old, so their C-14 has entirely gone. Anything older than about 60 000 y (ten half-lives leave under 0.1% of the C-14, too little to measure reliably) or younger than about 60 y (the drop is too small to measure).
  • Direction of errors. If a sample was contaminated with extra C-12, or the atmosphere had less C-14 when it lived, its activity per gram is lower than assumed and the calculated age is too high.
  • Always compare per gram: a 50 g sample giving 4.5 counts per minute is 0.09 min-1 g-1.
Worked example

Living wood gives 15 counts per minute per gram of carbon. A 50 g sample of carbon from an ancient beam gives 4.5 counts per minute (background already subtracted). Estimate the beam's age. Half-life of C-14 = 5730 y.

  1. Per gram: \( 4.5 / 50 = 0.090 \) min-1 g-1.
  2. \( A/A_0 = 0.090/15 = 0.0060 \). Number of half-lives \( n = \log_2(1/0.0060) = \ln(167)/\ln 2 = 7.38 \).
  3. \( t = 7.38 \times 5730 = 42\,300 \) y. (Equivalently \( t = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{A_0}{A} \) with \( k = \ln 2 / 5730 \).)

Forgetting to divide by 50 g gives \( A/A_0 = 0.30 \) and an age of about 10 000 y.

Concept check

Carbon from an ancient wooden object gives a corrected count rate of 11.0 min-1. The same mass of carbon from fresh wood of the same kind gives 15.6 min-1. The half-life of C-14 is 5730 y. The approximate age of the object is

\( A/A_0 = 11.0/15.6 = 0.705 \), which is \( (1/2)^{n} \) with \( n = \ln(15.6/11.0)/\ln 2 = 0.504 \) half-lives. \( t = 0.504 \times 5730 = 2900 \) y: D. A quick check: 0.705 is just under \( (1/2)^{1/2} = 0.707 \), so just over half a half-life. B is the linear estimate \( (1 - 0.705) \times 5730 \times 0.77 \); C is a rounding of "about a third of a half-life".

Concept check

Which of the following could be dated reliably by the carbon-14 method?

C: linen is plant fibre, once living, and 3000 y is about half a half-life, a comfortable fraction to measure. A never exchanged carbon with the atmosphere (use uranium-lead dating instead). B is over 50 half-lives old: essentially no C-14 remains. D has lost only 0.2% of its C-14, too small a change to detect.

Concept check

Why can the carbon-14 method not be used to find the age of a living person?

C. The method measures time since carbon exchange stopped, which for a living person has not happened. B is a real limitation for very young objects but not the reason a living person cannot be dated at all; A and D are false.

GDating rocks, and disposing of waste

  • Uranium-lead dating. Rocks contain no living carbon, but uranium-238 (half-life \( 4.47 \times 10^{9} \) y) decays through a series to stable lead-206. Comparing the amounts of parent and daughter in a rock gives the time since the rock solidified. Meteorites and the oldest Earth rocks give the age of the Earth as about \( 4.5 \times 10^{9} \) y. Each U-238 nucleus that reaches Pb-206 has emitted 8 α particles, so trapped helium counts decays too.
  • Radioactive waste. Low-level waste (old smoke detectors, tracer syringes, contaminated gloves) cannot go to ordinary landfill. In Hong Kong it is stored at the Siu A Chau facility until its activity has fallen to a safe level; clinical waste is labelled as radioactive. Long-lived, high-level waste from reactors is stored in shielded, cooled containers for decades and then buried deep in stable rock.
Worked example

A rock is found to contain 15 uranium-238 atoms for every 8 helium atoms trapped in it. Each U-238 to Pb-206 decay releases 8 α particles, which become helium atoms. Estimate the age of the rock. Half-life of U-238 = \( 4.5 \times 10^{9} \) y.

  1. 8 helium atoms mean one uranium nucleus has decayed. So for every 16 original U atoms, 15 remain: \( N/N_0 = 15/16 \).
  2. \( (1/2)^{n} = 15/16 \), \( n = \log_2(16/15) = 0.093 \) half-lives.
  3. \( t = 0.093 \times 4.5 \times 10^{9} = 4.2 \times 10^{8} \) y.

Book 5 · Ch.226.3 Radiation safety
Map 26.1 26.2 26.3 Summary

26.3

Radiation safety

Why ionizing radiation harms living tissue, how the harm is measured (dose, in sieverts, is not the same as activity, in becquerels), what typical doses look like, and the handling rules that keep dose low. Most exam marks here are for giving a reason with each precaution.

Learning objectives

Students should be able to:

  • represent radiation equivalent dose using the unit sievert (Sv)

    2026/32 MC

  • discuss potential hazards of ionizing radiation and the ways to minimise the radiation dose absorbed

    2026/32 MC2015/32 MC2021/9 LQ

  • suggest safety precautions in handling radioactive sources

    2015/32 MC2014/10 LQ

AWhy ionizing radiation is dangerous

Mechanism

α, β, γ and X-rays carry enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms. In living tissue this breaks up molecules in cells, in particular DNA. A cell may die, or its damaged DNA may make it divide uncontrollably, which is cancer. Damage to reproductive cells can be passed to offspring. The effects are cumulative: many small doses add up.

Source outside the bodySource inside the body (breathed in, swallowed, through a wound)
αLittle risk: stopped by a few centimetres of air or by the dead outer layer of skin.Most dangerous: all its energy is dumped within a fraction of a millimetre of tissue, giving intense ionization at that spot.
βSome risk: penetrates about a centimetre into tissue, so can burn skin and damage the eye.Dangerous: ionizes the tissue around where it collects, less intensely than α but over a few millimetres.
γMost dangerous of the three: passes through the body and can irradiate every organ from a distance.Still irradiates the whole body, but most of the energy passes out again, so the local damage is less than α.
  • Radioactive material gets inside the body as dust on food or fingers, as contaminated food and drink, and as radon, a radioactive gas.
  • Radon-222 is a member of the uranium-238 decay series and seeps out of rocks, soil and concrete. Indoors it accumulates, especially in poorly ventilated rooms and lower floors of buildings. Breathed in, it and its α-emitting daughters lodge in the lungs, where the α ionizes lung tissue directly: hence lung cancer in uranium miners. Radon is the largest single contributor to natural background dose (about 1.5 mSv per year). The remedy is ventilation.
  • "Hot springs rich in radon cure disease" is not supported by the physics: α from radon in the body ionizes healthy cells at random, which is damage, not treatment. Radiotherapy works only because the source is targeted at a tumour.
  • Higher activity does not automatically mean more harm. The harm depends also on the type of radiation, whether the source is inside or outside the body, how far away it is, how long the exposure lasts, and what shielding is between.

Concept check

A source emits both α and γ radiation. Which radiation is the greater hazard (i) if the source is swallowed, (ii) if the source is held against the skin?

Inside the body the strongly ionizing α, with all its energy absorbed locally, is the greater hazard. On the skin the α is stopped by the dead outer layer and does nothing, while the γ passes into the body. B. C reverses the logic; A and D ignore the location.

Concept check

Sample X has a higher activity than sample Y. Does X necessarily cause more biological harm to a person nearby?

B. Activity is what the source emits; harm depends on what the body absorbs and how. A weak α source swallowed can do more harm than a stronger γ source across the room. D still ignores distance, time and shielding; C is irrelevant to harm.

Concept check

Radon gas is a greater hazard to the lungs than to any other organ because

C. Radon is an α emitter; α is harmless outside the body and most harmful inside. Being a gas gets it inside, to the lungs specifically. D is true of radon but explains where it collects in a room, not why it harms the lungs. B is false (Rn-222 half-life is 3.8 days); A has the wrong radiation.

BActivity is emitted; dose is absorbed

Definitions

Absorbed dose is the radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue. It increases with the strength of the source, the time of exposure and closeness to the source. The equivalent dose (also called effective dose) weights the absorbed dose for how damaging each radiation is, and for how sensitive the tissue is:

\[ \text{equivalent dose} = \text{absorbed dose} \times W_{\text{radiation}} \times W_{\text{tissue}} \]

Unit: the sievert (Sv). One sievert is a large dose, so everyday values are quoted in millisieverts (mSv).

Radiation weighting factor \( W_{\text{radiation}} \)Tissue weighting factor \( W_{\text{tissue}} \) (examples)
α: 20
β, γ, X-rays: 1		gonads 0.20 · stomach 0.12 · colon 0.12 · liver 0.05 · oesophagus 0.05 · skin 0.01
  • The factor of 20 for α says that, joule for joule, α does about twenty times the biological damage of β or γ, because it deposits its energy so densely. Once the weighting has been applied, 1 Sv from α and 1 Sv from γ mean the same biological effect; that is the whole point of the unit.
  • Two people at different distances from the same source receive different doses from the same activity. Dose is about the receiver; activity is about the source.
Typical equivalent doses
Dental X-ray0.01 mSv
Chest X-ray check0.02 mSv
Flight Hong Kong to New York (cosmic rays at altitude)0.06 mSv
Watching television0.02 mSv per year
Cosmic rays at sea level0.3 mSv per year
Food and drink (mainly potassium-40)0.4 mSv per year
Radon in the home1.5 mSv per year
Total background, Hong Kong (about 80% natural, 20% artificial, mostly medical)2.4 mSv per year
CT scan10 mSv
Smoking 20 cigarettes a day (polonium-210 in tobacco)36 mSv per year
Whole-body dose received in a short timeEffect
500 mSvabnormal blood cell counts
1000 mSv (1 Sv)radiation sickness: nausea, vomiting
4000 mSvinternal bleeding, hair loss; death possible
6000 mSvfatal within weeks without treatment
10 000 mSv and abovefatal within weeks; much higher doses kill within days or hours
  • These are acute effects of a large dose all at once. Small doses spread over years produce no immediate symptoms but raise the lifetime risk of cancer; there is no dose known to be completely safe, which is why exposure is kept as low as reasonably achievable.
  • Limits (over and above natural background and medical procedures): 1 mSv per year for members of the public, 20 mSv per year for radiation workers.

Concept check

Which unit is used to measure the radiation equivalent dose received by a patient undergoing radiotherapy?

A. Becquerel measures the activity of the source; joule measures energy without reference to mass, radiation type or tissue; W m-2 is an intensity. Only the sievert folds in the biological weighting.

Concept check

Background in Hong Kong is about 2.4 mSv per year. A chest X-ray gives about 0.02 mSv and smoking 10 cigarettes a day gives about 18 mSv per year. In one year Sam smokes 5 cigarettes a day and has three chest X-rays. His total equivalent dose for the year is about

Smoking: half of 18 is 9 mSv. X-rays: \( 3 \times 0.02 = 0.06 \) mSv. Background: 2.4 mSv. Total \( 2.4 + 9 + 0.06 = 11.46 \approx 11.5 \) mSv, C. B is his dose above background; D uses 10 cigarettes a day; A forgets the smoking. Note that the cigarettes contribute far more than the X-rays.

Concept check

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

  1. The biological effect of radiation depends only on the energy absorbed, not on the type of radiation or the organ.
  2. An equivalent dose of 1 Sv from an α source and 1 Sv from a γ source cause about the same biological effect.
  3. A dose of 1 Sv received in a short time is harmless.

(1) is false: that is why the weighting factors exist. (2) is true: the weighting for α (20) has already been applied in arriving at 1 Sv, so equal sieverts mean equal effect. (3) is false: 1 Sv at once causes radiation sickness. Answer B.

CKeeping the dose low

PrincipleWhy it works
Time: keep exposure shortDose accumulates with time. Plan the work so that sources are out of their containers for as little time as possible.
Distance: stay far awayRadiation spreads out in all directions from a small source, so intensity falls off rapidly with distance (roughly as \( 1/r^{2} \) for γ). α does not even reach you beyond a few centimetres.
Shielding: put dense material betweenLead or thick concrete stops β and greatly weakens γ. Wood or a thin aluminium box will not do for a γ source; a dense material is needed.
PrecautionReason
Store sources in a labelled lead-lined container, locked away, and return them immediately after useShielding, and minimum time out of the container
Handle with long forceps or tongs; never touch a source; never point it at anyoneDistance; keeps the source away from fingers and eyes and the beam away from people
Wear gloves, protective clothing and a lead apron where appropriate; wash hands after; no eating or drinking in the laboratoryPrevents radioactive material entering the body, where α and β do most harm
Wear a film badge or dosimeterRecords the dose received so exposure can be monitored and workers rotated. It does not reduce the dose
Only trained, authorised persons handle sources; use remote handling (robot arms, thick windows) for strong sourcesTime and distance for the people who face the largest doses
Label and store radioactive waste separately (for example contaminated syringes after a tracer test)Prevents contamination of others and of ordinary refuse
For patients: keep X-ray and CT examinations to those that are needed; shield parts of the body not being imagedMedical procedures are the main artificial contribution to dose
Worked example

Polonium-210, an α emitter with a half-life of 138 days, was used in a notorious poisoning. (a) Explain why a Po-210 source is far more dangerous swallowed than carried in a sealed container in a pocket. (b) Find its decay constant in s-1. (c) After how long would the activity in a contaminated object have fallen to a quarter of its initial value? (d) Why could traces still be detected weeks afterwards?

  1. (a) α is stopped by the container wall (or by skin), so outside the body the dose is negligible. Swallowed, the α deposits all its energy in the surrounding tissue, giving a very high, heavily weighted (\( W = 20 \)) dose.
  2. (b) \( k = \ln 2 / T_{1/2} = 0.693 / (138 \times 24 \times 3600) = 5.81 \times 10^{-8} \) s-1.
  3. (c) A quarter is two half-lives: \( 2 \times 138 = 276 \) d.
  4. (d) A 138-day half-life is long compared with a few weeks, so most of the Po-210 was still undecayed and still emitting.

Concept check

When performing an experiment with a radioactive source, can the radiation dose received be reduced by

  1. planning the experiment so that the handling time is shorter?
  2. storing the source in a lead container when it is not in use?
  3. wearing a film badge?

(1) is the time principle and (2) is shielding. A film badge (3) only records the dose already received; it does nothing to reduce it. Answer B.

Concept check

A school stores a γ source in a box. Which box material gives the best protection, and why?

C. γ is only weakened, never fully stopped; the thicker and denser the absorber, the more it is weakened, and lead is the practical choice. B is true only for α and β. A confuses electrical with radiation shielding; D is false: γ passes through wood or aluminium almost unchanged.

Write it out

A technician has to move a small γ source from its store to a demonstration bench and back. State four precautions the technician should take and give the reason for each. (4 marks)

  1. Carry the source in its lead container and take it out only at the bench: shielding, and minimum time exposed.
  2. Handle it with long tongs and keep it pointed away from people: distance, and no one in the beam.
  3. Plan the demonstration beforehand so the source is out for the shortest possible time: dose accumulates with time.
  4. Wear a film badge (and gloves; wash hands afterwards): so that the dose received is recorded, and so that no radioactive material is carried to the mouth.

Any four precaution-with-reason pairs. A precaution without its reason scores half.

4Traps that cost marks

Decayed nuclei are still there

They have become the daughter. Mass does not vanish; the sample becomes a parent-daughter mixture. "Amount decayed" is \( N_0 - N \), not \( N \).

Subtract background, then halve, then add it back

Half-life is read from the corrected count rate. On an uncorrected graph, read the time at (corrected/2 + background).

Long half-life is not weak

\( A = kN \): a large sample of a long-lived nuclide can out-emit a small sample of a short-lived one. Compare activities, not half-lives.

Half the time is not half the loss

After half a half-life 71% remains, not 75%. Decay is exponential; use \( (1/2)^{t/T} \) or \( e^{-kt} \) for any \( t \), including non-integers.

"By" one third is not "to" one third

Decreasing by one third leaves 2/3. Decreasing to one third leaves 1/3. The times differ by a factor of about 2.7.

k is not the activity

\( k \) is the probability of decay per nucleus per second, constant for the nuclide. \( A \) is the whole sample's decays per second and falls with time.

Half-life reasons come in pairs

Long enough to do the job; short enough not to linger (tracers) or long enough to stay steady (gauges, detectors, therapy machines). Give both halves.

Irradiated is not radioactive

Food, instruments and X-rayed patients absorb energy, not radioactive atoms. Only contamination with radioactive material makes something radioactive.

Activity falls, penetrating power does not

An old source emits fewer particles per second; each particle is as penetrating as ever. A film badge records dose; it does not reduce it.

A gauge relies on the radiation being partly absorbed (penetrating power). A smoke detector relies on α ionizing the air. Dating relies on the half-life never changing. A. B swaps the first two; D forgets that the gauge count is about penetration.

In 4 h, P has 4 half-lives (factor 1/16) and Q has 2 (factor 1/4). With \( A_Q = 6.0 \times 10^{6} - A_P \): \( A_P/16 + (6.0 \times 10^{6} - A_P)/4 = 6.0 \times 10^{5} \). Multiply by 16: \( A_P + 4(6.0 \times 10^{6}) - 4A_P = 9.6 \times 10^{6} \), so \( 3A_P = 1.44 \times 10^{7} \), \( A_P = 4.8 \times 10^{6} \) Bq: C. A is the answer for Q.

Two samples P and Q of different radionuclides are found to have the same corrected count rate at \( t = 10 \) min. P's count rate falls more steeply than Q's. Which of the following is correct at \( t = 10 \) min?

Steeper fall means a larger fraction decays per minute: larger \( k \), shorter half-life. Equal activities with \( A = kN \) means the sample with larger \( k \) has smaller \( N \): B. A is the common error of equating count rate with amount.
